Hon. Warren Allmand (Notre-Dame-de-Grace-Lachine
East): Mr. Speaker, on January 1 the Mulroney Government robbed thousands of Canadians of their hard-earned unemployment insurance benefits by counting early retirement pensions as income. This was done despite a legion of protests, pleas, and petitions. Approximately one year ago the Government announced this measure, and because of this advance notice it believes that Canadians should be able to adjust to it and accept it. This is not the case. There was little publicity and little formal consultation.
Every day new individuals and groups are finding out that this measure affects them and cruelly reduces their forced early retirement income. Worse still, the Government is forcing certain employees, such as members of the Canadian Armed Forces who must retire early, to pay unemployment insurance premiums but will not let them collect the benefits.
The Government has appointed the Forget Commission to examine the entire unemployment insurance system. Why does it not show some commonsense by suspending this harsh measure and referring it to the Forget Commission where it can be studied in the context of other possible changes?

subtopic: CANADIAN'S DEATH IN JAMAICA-ALLEGED LACK OF ASSISTANCE FROM CANADA'S HIGH COMMISSION
CANADIAN'S DEATH IN JAMAICA-ALLEGED LACK OF ASSISTANCE FROM CANADA'S HIGH COMMISSION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to bring to the attention of this House a matter of immense tragedy. A young constituent of mine was killed in an accident in Jamaica last Thursday morning. To the family, friends, and to me, the loss is enormous and personal. To our country and to the
family, however, the grief has been transformed into agony by the thorough incompetence and uncaring attitude of Canada's High Commission in Jamaica.
During the past four days no one from our Commission travelled to the scene of the accident or to the hospital where this young Canadian lay. The father and a friend of the deceased received no assistance from the High Commission on arrival in Montego Bay and were forced to search out their lost kin in the basement of a hospital in Savanna la Mar. Throughout the day yesterday no duty officer could be raised to assist, despite repeated efforts by the family, myself, and External Affairs here in Ottawa.
I wish to thank those staff at External Affairs here in Ottawa who kindly assisted me and the family over the past few days, including the Under-Secretary of State, Mr. Taylor, who came sincerely to the task at 2 a.m. this morning.
I am confident that all Members of this House share in the grief of the family, and also share in the wisdom of recalling every member of Canada's High Commission to Jamaica to Ottawa for retraining in the basic elements of human decency. As the father, Warner Funk, Sr., said to me moments ago from Jamaica: "No parent should ever have to undergo such horror again".

subtopic: GENERAL MOTORS PLANT IN SCARBOROUGH-VAN SALES TO UNITED STATES
GENERAL MOTORS PLANT IN SCARBOROUGH-VAN SALES TO UNITED STATES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, last week the one millionth van rolled off the assembly line in the Scarborough plant of General Motors. That plant manufactures vans for sale throughout the entire continent of North America and, as a result, provides employment for 2,400 production workers plus 250 administrative staff. Its magnificent record of production and sales shows what can happen when Canadian labour and management work together, but it also shows what can happen when Canada and the United States work together.
I ask the House, how many of those 2,650 people would have employment if that plant could sell vans only to Canadians? How many more Canadians who benefit from General Motors spin-offs would have work but for the Auto Pact? The success of that agreement points the way of the future. It is the way of gaining guaranteed access to a market large enough to provide Canadians with opportunities that our 25 million people cannot provide on our own.
The Government has shown vision and courage by inviting the United States to join Canada in trade discussions which may expand this kind of opportunity in other industries, and this kind of opportunity for all Canadians. Almost 20 years ago one of the key players making that Auto Pact possible was the then Prime Minister, the Right Hon. Lester Pearson. One could wish his Party had the vision today that he had then.
February 3, 1986

Mr. Speaker, two weeks ago the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Wise) announced our party's new long-term dairy policy, to be renewed for five years, including the subsidy program.
Dairy farmers in my riding are very happy with this decision which demonstrates the Government's formal commitment to this vital sector of our economy. The policy will also help to boost the recovery of the agricultural sector among the expropriated farmers of Mirabel. Canadian dairy producers still remember the unilateral cuts in quotas made by our predecessors, which caused many new dairy operations to go out of business.
Today I would like to remind the House that the dairy policy was the result of consultation between farmers and various parties in the industry, and that without this consensus and commitment to regulate production, no dairy policy would have been possible.
Considering their commitment and their sensitivity to the public's well-being farmers deserve our admiration, especially after surviving fifteen years of Liberal Government, which is quite a feat, Mr. Speaker, for an industry as regulated as the Canadian dairy industry.

subtopic: DEMAND FOR RESIGNATION OF DEPUTY PRIME MINISTER
DEMAND FOR RESIGNATION OF DEPUTY PRIME MINISTER

Mr. Speaker, the time-honoured tradition of Parliament requires that every Member feel free to speak out in caucus without having to fear that his or her words are being intercepted by another political Party. The violation of this tradition by the Deputy Prime Minister (Mr. Nielsen) casts into question his ability to function in his current dual roles as Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of National Defence. Imagine what our allies must be saying about the possibility of interception that could exist on matters of national and international security.
What must the country think of a man who systematically eavesdropped accidentally every Wednesday for five months? subtopic: HAITI-CALL FOR CUT IN CANADIAN AID
HAITI-CALL FOR CUT IN CANADIAN AID
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, Canadians have been appalled to hear of the carnage over the weekend in Haiti. There are reports of between 50 and 100 people being killed and many more injured in the anti-government demonstrations. Many Canadians would be even more appalled if they thought that their tax dollars were helping the repulsive regime of Jean-Claude Duvalier to maintain its grip on power.
Between Baby Doc and his father, the Duvalier family has tyrannized Haiti for 30 years. In the last 10 years Canadian aid has amounted to some $87 million, $8 million of that in the fiscal year 1984-85. With what result? The plight of the Haitian people is worse than ever. The flow of refugees to our country and others continues.
Baby Doc Duvalier is a cancerous growth on the Caribbean region and clearly has no intention of improving the desperate lot of his people. Until we see some willingness to respect human rights and democracy in Haiti, Canada should cut off its foreign aid for all but the most dire emergencies. My call is echoed by Canada's Haitian community as well. Let us stop aiding tyranny in Haiti now.

Mr. Speaker, I realize this Chamber does not exactly dwell on good news and positive events but, if you will bear with me, I would like to spend a few moments bringing Members up to date on Expo 86 in my home province this year.
The television advertisements, the pamphlets and posters and brochures cannot begin to capture the excitement of what is about to happen in Vancouver this May through October.
Even the naysayers are surprised at the success of Expo 86 to date. The site itself is sold out. An unprecedented 8 million visits to the Fair have been sold three months before the door is even open.
On Vancouver Island our Expo 86 will begin on May I, when Prince Charles and Diana, the Princess of Wales, will visit Victoria and Nanaimo. Together, Expo 86 and the concurrent Islands 86 celebration will host the largest international event on this Continent between now and the end of this century.

February 3, 1986
This weekend Members of Parliament from across Canada will get a preview look at Expo 86 and experience a Canada we have never experienced before.
From Canada Place on the harbour to the Expo site itself, "from Bonavista to Vancouver Island," as the song says, we are about to discover what is good about this nation, what is exciting about this nation, and what we have to offer the world. Expo 86, - what the world is coming to. The people of British Columbia have much to be proud of.
Hear, hear!

Mr. Speaker, by the end of today's Question Period, that is, in about 50 minutes, the Canadian Government will have increased its deficit by $16,346,000. In a single hour, the Government will have spent 0.5 per cent of its total annual revenue from taxpayers across Canada.
Mr. Speaker, will this Question Period be put to good use by Opposition Members? Are they going to consider these financial constraints we are subject to or are they going to waste the time of the House on trivialities?
Mr. Speaker, today's editorial in the Globe and Mail appears under the title "A budget for less debt". That, Mr. Speaker, is what it is all about. Hon. Members are here in the House to legislate and administer, and their main instrument is the Budget. Let us focus all our energies and our sense of purpose on this area, and Canada's economic renewal, which has been well under way since September 1984, will continue to progress for the benefit of us all.
That should be the objective of all the elected Members of this House.

subtopic: TOXIC CHEMICALS IN ST. CLAIR RIVER
TOXIC CHEMICALS IN ST. CLAIR RIVER
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, if the Government of Canada thinks that it can clean up the past and present activities on the St. Clair River through a yet to be introduced Environmental Contaminants Act, it is dreaming in colour. Existing toxic chemicals in the river-bed, sewer outfalls, leaching from dump sites, existing and ongoing sources of pollution cannot be dealt with through legislation not in the books. The St. Clair is an international river. The Government
of Canada has a responsibility under the Great Lakes Water Quality Agreement to clean up the situation.
The Government has several instruments at its disposal. It could reinstate the two-year accelerated write offs under the Income Tax Act, an important incentive to industry to install modern treatment equipment, separate sewers, modernize monitoring systems, and ensure that the highest standards of waste treatment are applied. It could offer a special program for municipalities such as Sarnia to provide financial assistance for the installation of equipment and facilities for the best possible treatment of residential, commercial, and industrial waste waters which pass through municipal sewer systems. It could even create a super fund with interested provincial Governments, to remove toxic wastes from dumps and therefore remove the source of future problems at leaking dumps.
To restore the confidence of people living alongside the St. Clair River, the federal Minister of the Environment (Mr. McMillan) has to act and move swiftly with the momentum created by the St. Clair River-

Mr. Speaker, the deficit is the biggest single problem facing Canadians today. The deficit has become a cancer; it has entered our system and is spreading its disease throughout the country. There is virtually no day that goes by which does not remind us of how oppressive the deficit has become. It affects interest rates, thus hitting every home owner, every consumer, and every business person. It affects the funds available for social concerns and thus ultimately threatens every social program in Canada. It affects government plans and options, as was demonstrated when the drought hit many farmers this spring and summer. We were faced with a desperate situation and were forced to cope with a crisis, with scarce, borrowed resources.
I believe that three things must be done to allow us to rid ourselves of this dealdy, ever-growing weight upon us. The first is that the spending and raising of Canadian tax dollars have to be seen as related, working together. This means that we need a regularized structure in Parliament, tying the Estimates to the Budget and vice versa. Second, the Government of Canada needs to take many of the tough decisions required to reduce the deficit. Finally, the Canadian people must get involved by offering their help and energies to beat this problem. The deficit is too large a problem to be left in the hands of a few. It is a problem for all Canadians to tackle.
February 3, 1986

maintopic: NATIONAL SOCCER TEAM-REFUSAL OF UNITED STATES CLUBS TO RELEASE PLAYERS
NATIONAL SOCCER TEAM-REFUSAL OF UNITED STATES CLUBS TO RELEASE PLAYERS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, all of Canada is proud of our National Soccer Team which is going to Mexico later this year to participate for the first time ever in a World Cup Tournament. Its success so far is a tribute to a concerted effort by so many individuals associated with the Canadian Soccer Association, and it has been made even greater by the fact that they have had to overcome as many obstacles off the field as on it.
The latest problem centres around the refusal of the Major Indoor Soccer League in the United States to release our Canadian stars to play with their national team in warm-up matches. In soccer all over the world it is a matter of pride for a club to have its players selected for a national team, and they willingly allow their players leave to participate in international soccer. But not in North America. Here the dollar rules, and club owners are afraid of losing attendance if their stars are released from time to time. It is a sign of immaturity which must be overcome if soccer is ever to be successful in North America.
I also have to wonder if the same reluctance would be shown if the players were to be released to play for a U.S. national team. It is time for the Sports Minister to offer his assistance in resolving this matter to allow our team, all of it, the time for practice and development which it so richly deserves.

subsubtopic: DIFFERENCE BETWEEN INTEREST RATE ON CANADA SAVINGS BONDS AND INTEREST RATE ON TREASURY BILLS- GOVERNMENT POSITION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on September 4, 1984, when the Conservatives came to power, the preferred rate was the same in Canada and the United States. Today, there is a difference of 200 base points.
My question to the Minister of Finance is as follows: The savings bonds issued by the Canadian Government last November pay 8.5 per cent interest to holders. Since February 1, the bonds are redeemable without penalty, so that Canadians can cash them. Now, the interest rate on one-year Treasury bills is almost 11 per cent. My question for the Minister of Finance is quite simple. Does he intend to increase the interest on savings bonds, so that Canadians can get the same rate of interest on their savings that banks and trust companies get on one-year Treasury bills?

subsubtopic: DIFFERENCE BETWEEN INTEREST RATE ON CANADA SAVINGS BONDS AND INTEREST RATE ON TREASURY BILLS- GOVERNMENT POSITION

Mr. Speaker, 1 think the Hon. Member knows, he being a former Minister of Finance in the Quebec Government, that there is a lot of instability in the international market-place. speechtext:

The Government has the same rate on Canada Savings Bonds for a full year because they are a different type of investment instrument. They can be cashed at any time. Canada Savings Bonds have a degree of stability to them that provide the investor with a lot more safety in holding that investment. For that reason the difference in interest rates is warranted.

The House resumed consideration of the motion of Mr. Caccia:
That this House condemns the Government for its failure to recognize the importance attributed by Canadians to toxic chemicals in water and other elements of the environment.

Mr. Speaker, in speaking to the motion today I want to begin by expressing a word of commendation to my friend the Hon. Member for Davenport (Mr. Caccia) for bringing to the attention of this House a matter that is timely, relevant and urgent. The Hon. Member for Davenport is certainly one of the most respected environmentalists in Canada today. 1 believe that my Party is fortunate to have him as our spokesperson and critic on environmental issues.
Canadians today in all parts of the country are deeply concerned about the quality of our environment. They look to the federal Government for leadership in the resolution of environmental problems and the preservation of a very rich natural heritage that we still possess. Inaction by the federal Government cannot be excused on the basis that there is a jurisdictional overlap between the provinces and the federal Government when it comes to environmental issues.
Canadians expect strong leadership from the federal Government. As the Member for Davenport pointed out in introducing this motion they are not at the present time getting the leadership that they expect and deserve. Inaction cannot be excused either because neglect of our environment may sometimes be profitable in the short run. Canadians know that environmental degradation inevitably harms the economy in the long run. For example, acid rain harms tourism and buildings. If we have poor forest management it leads to a shortage of wood. The effects of pollutants in air and water causes health problems. That, Sir, leads to absenteeism and much higher costs for our health care system.
There are many environmental problems in this country, Mr. Speaker, which really are the result of one sector of society trying to avoid paying the costs of waste disposal or of sustaining a particular resource. They just try to avoid it. These costs will not go away. They are simply passed on to others, another sector of society or, even more seriously, they are passed on to future generations.
The debate today in this House concerns the toxic chemicals issue, and no one should be misled. The task of intervening by the federal Government to control toxic chemicals which will find their way into our environment is an enormous task. Ours has been described as being a chemical age. Probably that is more to be regretted than it is to be cheered. We know that modern industry today uses some 60,000 chemicals in a very wide variety of processes. Many of these products that are used are new, they have been synthesized within this century.

February 3, 1986
Supply
For the most part we have only very limited data concerning their long-term environmental and health impacts. We just don't know enough about them.
There are 1,000 new chemicals that are utilized annually, but there is no comprehensive legislation to monitor and control them. This is not to suggest that the federal Government in the past has been inactive or unconcerned-not at all. The federal Government has six Acts regarding toxic chemical management. There is the Environmental Contaminants Act of 1976, the Clean Air Act, the Canada Water Act, the Ocean Dumping Control Act, Section 33 of the Fisheries Act, and, of course, the Migratory Birds Convention Act. In addition to that there are another 30 related federal Acts; that is, in a variety of statutes there are aspects that direct themselves to environmental matters. For the provinces there is a total of another 97 Acts that deal with specific aspects of toxic chemicals.
That is impressive, but all of this legislation has not proved successful. It has not solved our pollution problems resulting from toxic chemical disposal. I wonder why that is, Sir? The reason it seems-and the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Epp) referred to it in his speech-is that monitoring, regulating, and controlling have not kept pace with the development of new chemicals. Regulation development requires a political commitment, the exercise of strong political will and the direction of the necessary financial resources in order that we can keep pace.
The Minister of National Health and Welfare admitted this morning that those resources are not available. Does that mean that we should therefore conclude that there is not a political commitment on the part of this Government to face up to the big challenge of dealing with toxic chemicals entering our environment? There is reason to be suspicious that there is not that commitment.
As my friend from Davenport pointed out, the toxicology centre in Guelph, which had an allocation of $6 million at its disposal and was destined to become a centre of excellence in North America attracting the best of scientists, has ceased to function. We know that an important toxic chemical research program with respect to the Niagara River, which had an allocation of some $2.5 million a year, has been cancelled. We know the National Research Council was doing important research on toxic chemicals. There is no longer money available for it to carry on that work.
The key issue is that chemicals continue to be used in great abundance in our society. New ones are regularly introduced, but are done so without an adequate assessment program to deal with the risks they may pose.
The simple fact, and Hon. Members have to face up to it, is that Canada lacks an effective control and assessment policy for chemical usage and disposal. What does that mean, Mr. Speaker? It means we are gambling that there will be no ill effects either to the environment or to human health when one
of these new chemicals is used and disposed of in some unacceptable way.
It is frequently charged that in Canada most chemicals have not been tested adequately to determine their toxicity, how they effect ecosystems and how they interact with other chemicals. Consequently, citizens of Canada, those who we represent here, are raising numerous questions about the safety of drinking water and the risks involved in the eating of fish.
There is a great deal of disagreement, of course, even amount experts about the impact of toxic chemicals on the environment. Some very clear signals, however, and problems do exist. The big proportion of fish with cancerous tumours that have been taken from the polluted areas of the Great Lakes is a very clear signal that we have a water quality problem.
A three-year study was undertaken by Environment Canada in co-operation with the Government of the Northwest Territories. It revealed high concentrations of certain agricultural and industrial chemicals, including PCBs, in polar bears. The very fact that PCBs and other toxic chemicals have been found in northern Canada-supposed to be our pristine wilderness- indicates that we have to rethink our approach to these toxic chemicals, to manage them better throughout their life cycle and to prevent them from finding their way into the environment affecting human health and wildlife as well.
We do not yet fully understand how these toxical chemicals got into the North. There can be no dispute here about federal responsibility. There is a federal responsibility to develop the best possible means of preventing that from happening. Our well being is intimately connected to the quality of this nation's air, water and soil. For example, PCBs and mercury were widely used for a long period of time and thought to be safe until scientists suddenly discovered that they have harmful effects.
Let me just take the case of mercury. The Indian people who live in northwestern Ontario in the communities of White Dog and Grassy Narrows are today tragic reminders of the sad fact that we did not carry out our responsibilities to guarantee their health and safety.
What we have, and the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Epp) admitted it this morning, is an ad hoc process by Environment Canada and the Department of National Health and Welfare in assessing and controlling the 60,000 chemicals now on the market. That is not adequate to protect the health and the environment of Canadians.
Our neighbour to the south does not have a great reputation for environmental concerns in many areas-
Putting it mildly.

Putting it mildly, yes. Nevertheless, if you take a look at the Americans' Environmental Protection Agency, it has a much more sophisticated and advanced process for monitoring, regulating and controlling toxic chemicals than do we. The Americans have clearly defined stages. They have decision-making criteria to identify and regulate hazardous
February 3, 1986

chemicals. Canada does not have a system like that and it needs one.
On August 9, 1985, the Aboriginal Council of British Columbia wrote to the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development (Mr. Crombie) supporting the efforts of the Kitsumkalum Indian Band Council in its fight to stop the herbicidal spraying of a chemical known as Garlon Ester 4. This case illustrates so well the need to prevent toxic chemicals from entering lakes, rivers and ground waters. There seems to be an absence of any strong federal leadership. In fact, the federal Government in this case, it is sad to say, was the culprit.
The previous Minister of the Environment, who has now left the Cabinet altogether and never really was regarded as much of a champion of our biosphere nevertheless acknowledged that considerable experience had been gained in coping with chemicals in Canada since the passage of the Environmental Contaminants Act of 1976. She indicated that much more had to be done. She called for, and she should be given credit for this, a comprehensive management plan. She said:
Toxic chemicals must be and will be safely managed in Canada.
That is why my hon. friend and colleague from Davenport has called for this debate. We in this Party want to see the Government bring in such a comprehensive management plan. Will it do so? If so, when?
No one questions that there are some chemical substances that are of value to society; that is not the issue here today. It must be recognized that their widespread and unregulated use poses very great risks to human health and to the environment. Industrial societies such as ours are steadily increasing the potential exposure of citizens to chemicals which can cause cancer, birth defects, blood diseases, miscarriages, nervous disorders and damages to the liver, the kidney and the genes. All of the chemicals in use today will enter into the environment in one way or another. Too little is known about the effects of chemicals on living beings.
Possibly, hundreds of these chemicals pose no serious risks at all, but others are unquestionably dangerous. The federal Government is responsible for overseeing that we have national water safety standards in the country. It should be in a position to ensure for every Canadian, no matter where that citizen lives, the right to clean, safe drinking water. The federal Government should have the force of law behind it to order industries to have recycling centres for industrial discharge.
Think about it for a moment, Mr. Speaker. The concept that discharge of these chemicals is acceptable because they dilute in water surely has to be considered irresponsible. I would like to use an authority in this regard. I quote the words of Dr. Wilkinson of Carleton University who gave testimony before the Pearse Commission. He said:
Toxic chemical waste ought not to be a topic of water management-but it is. We do need control of chemicals from creation to disposal. Storage in the ecosphere through dilution is irresponsible.

I think all Members in the House will agree that the emphasis has to be on prevention. The Government of Canada must have the power to prevent toxics from entering lakes, rivers and groundwater. If we have to rely on remedial measures, then we know that they are always expensive. They will be much more expensive than a systematic program of pollution prevention. Once a toxic chemical has been dispersed into the environment, it is usually difficult, or it may even be impossible, to clean it up.
I conclude by saying that this is an important debate. Its purpose is to stress, to elaborate and to emphasize the point that Canada needs a better system to assess and control toxic chemicals so that our citizens can be assured that their health, their safety and their concern for good environment is not constantly, daily, at threat.

Mr. Speaker, I think that if we want to be consistent ... I realize this is an Opposition day, but the motion could just as well have read: "That this House condemns the previous Government for its failure to recognize the importance attributed by Canadians to chemicals." The Hon. Member for Cochrane-Superior (Mr. Penner) referred to new toxic chemicals. He knows perfectly well-as he used to be on this side of the House, on the Government side-that it takes years to get a chemical certified for use.
I am aware of the Hon. Member's parliamentary record. I know that he is very interested in parliamentary procedure and reform, since he was a fairly active substitute member of the committee. The Hon. Member must remember those uncertain times of the urea formaldehyde foam insulation question, and in fact Canadians are still ... And we are still trying to deal with the difficult UFFI question. The Hon. Member will recall that at the time, approval of the product was . . . the Government of Canada had not been careful enough, and I think we can never be too careful. Now, is the Hon. Member for Cochrane-Superior prepared to admit in the House today that what is happening to us now-and environmental matters are very important to my constituents in Argenteuil-Papineau: there are a number of organizations whose concerns include the quality of air, water, forests, in fact the quality of life in general-is not the fault of this Government, because if we realize ... It seems it takes two or three years for a chemical to be certified for use.
The Standing Committee on Agriculture, and in fact I am not sure whether it is the Caucus Committee or the Standing Committee, at any rate the Committee met with the Canadian Manufacturers of Chemical Specialties Association and told us: It may take three years to get a product certified for the market.
So if the present regulations ... and what I want to ask him is: Does the Hon. Member recognize that the present regulations are a consequence of the previous legislation? It is as simple as that. That this Government has a tremendous

February 3, 1986
Supply
responsibility and is facing a tremendous challenge to deal with environmental matters and acid rain? That Canadians are not the only ones to blame for our acid rain, Mr. Speaker?
I would appreciate it if the Hon. Member for Cochrane-Superior would answer that, and if he would remember the days of UFFI. He must realize it is not easy for a government, and as my father used to say: It's easier to be on the outside looking into the ring than being in the ring yourself.

Mr. Speaker, I only have to say to the Hon. Member that the matter she raises is really peripheral. We are dealing here with a central problem. I was in this House when pollution matters and concern for the environment first became public policy issues. It happened in the late 1960s. Progressively, the Government became more and more concerned. A ministry was established, a Department was established and legislation was passed. Very frequently, as I indicated in my remarks, that legislation fell short of what citizens in the country expected from it.
The matter is simply this. We are dealing with a progressively serious problem. It is becoming more and more serious. So the issue now, as my hon. friend from Davenport has stressed by bringing this motion forward, is that the Government has been elected with a large majority to take leadership in a wide range of areas. Today in the House we are saying that one of the areas that must not be neglected is the area of toxic chemicals disposal. It is becoming a more and more serious problem, as represented by the questions which have been raised in the House about the St. Clair River. During previous administrations we had equally serious problems. We had to move on them; but there has to be a political will to do something about it and to commit the resources to those problems.
What concerns us is that there does not seem to be any clear statement of public policy from the Government on environmental issues. In fact, we on this side of the House seem to be getting the message that there is a drawback. If toxic chemicals are as serious as my hon. friend and experts in our community have indicated, then how can there be justification for major cut-backs when we ought to be allocating new resources to a comprehensive toxic chemical management program in the country? That is the challenge for this Government. 1 do not think that they are responding to the challenge, at least not to the satisfaction of either myself or the Hon. Member for Davenport.

Mr. Speaker, I think all of us in this House, no matter what side we sit on, are very sympathetic with the main thrust of the Hon. Member's comments. Obviously, all of us are most concerned about the environment. We are most concerned about toxic waste, toxic chemicals and, in particular, about toxic chemicals in our drinking water. Those are matters of common ground. I do not think that anyone is holier than thou in that respect.
The Hon. Member also knows from statements made by the Minister of the Environment (Mr. McMillan) in the House
last week that the Government has the intention within a very short period of time to introduce some very comprehensive changes to the Environmental Contaminants Act in order to make clear and to strengthen the whole thrust of the Government's enforcement and prevention policies in which the Hon. Member is interested.
The Hon. Member also knows that one of the main problems we face in dealing with the environment and the toxic chemical problem lies in the chemical dumps along the American side of the Niagara River, in particular those four infamous chemical dumps originally owned by the Hooker Chemical Company: the Love Canal, the Hyde Park dump, the S. Area dump and the 102 nd. Street dump. They are all along the American side of the Niagara River and they are all causing a great potential problem which somehow has to be dealt with. Those dumps have been there for a number of years. They did not just suddenly occur since September 4, 1984.
Since that time, of course, the present Government has been dealing with the American Government, the State of New York Government and with the chemical companies involved, trying to come to some sort of solution to the problem of cleaning up those dumps. The ultimate solution, of course, is to get rid of the chemicals, take them away and dispose of them somewhere else, and I mean actually dispose of them rather than just dump them in another site where they can cause the same sort of problem.
The present Government is doing something about that and it has been for some time. I am sure the Hon. Member has some thoughts of his own and is very disturbed by the fact that the Governments of which he was a part in the past were not able to do anything about those dumps. I hope he is prepared to admit to the House that the present Government is taking substantial action in that direction.
All of us, of course, are most interested in knowing what the Hon. Member would have done had he been the Minister of the Environment to clean up these dumps on the American side of the Niagara River. I hope the Hon. Member will help us with his own suggestions as to what he believes his Government should have done to clean up those dumps.

Mr. Speaker, first, no one disagrees for a moment that there has to be harmonization with our American friends in dealing with pollution problems that affect bodies of water which border our countries. Past administrations have always had an active policy of trying to seek that harmonization. But if my hon. friend, the Hon. Member for Davenport, were the Minister of the Environment, we would not have seen the $2.5 million cut in the toxic chemical research program for the Niagara River. I would like to ask my hon. friend how he justifies that.
Let me say on the third point that we have heard on many occasions a promise of an action plan, but I would like to see that action plan. We have not received the details of it as yet
February 3, 1986

and only have indications that it will be forthcoming. Part of the reason for this debate is to get that action plan brought forward much more quickly because it is urgent it be done soon.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Liberal Party
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I would like to ask a question of the Hon. Member for Cochrane-Superior (Mr. Penner). Some of us had the honour and privilege to visit northern Ontario and spend some time in some of its important industrial centres such as Dryden, Kapuskasing and Cochrane. Can the Hon. Member tell us if the people in his community are satisfied that at this time we as a Government are doing what should be done in terms of assessing possible damages of waste disposal and in terms of control and regulation? Are we making sure of the heritage we leave our children in northern Ontario, which is one of the largest and richest areas of the country? I am sure he will tell us that in his riding there are a lot of expectations and that we still have a lot to do.

Mr. Speaker, I mentioned in my remarks the alarm which had been created in the Indian communities of Whitedog and Grassy Narrows as a result of the mercury pollution which had come from the pulp and paper plant at Dryden, Ontario. It was some years later that the Government of Canada, in co-operation with the Government of Ontario- a Liberal and a Conservative administration-and in co-operation with the industry, put vast amounts of money into a program in northern Ontario for the pulp and paper industry which did two things; first, it modernized the industry and, second, it introduced the very latest pollution technology. We in northern Ontario at this time are benefiting from that multimillion dollar program which was put in place by two levels of Government, plus the industry. More than $1 billion was spent in a very short space of time. So we have done much in northern Ontario to clean up the act of our industry. But we are not so convinced that other industries in other parts of Canada are doing as well.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Resuming debate. The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of the Environment (Mr. Gurbin).
Hear, hear!

speakeroldname: Mr. G. M. Gurbin (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of the Environment):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of the Environment
speechtext:
I have at least one person who is interested in what I might say. I think the debate thus far is starting to take some focus and the question is becoming action and political will. I believe that is the bottom line of the remarks coming from the opposition today. It has been said, and I have mentioned it before, that this is an appropriate debate. There is no question about that. It is one which the Government welcomes. The Minister of the Environment (Mr. McMillan) would have dearly loved to have participated in the debate but he is out west today to make an announcement. I believe this is an example of action taken by the Government. The Hon. House Leader of the Opposition should perhaps take into account that the action the Hon. Member for Davenport (Mr. Caccia) was asking for several months ago in a Standing Order 22 is now being implemented in the announcement of
Supply
the four mountain parks plan. It will establish the arrangement between Parks Canada and the four mountain parks, with which most of us in Canada are very familiar and which are such a natural attribute and heritage to all Canadians. It will be an umbrella agreement, in co-operation with the people in the area and with the 3,200 organizations and individuals taking part in the formation of that plan.
The comments to which I would like to respond first are those comments made by the critic for the New Democratic Party this morning. He made two points to do with this Government and with what, in his mind, would be our difficulty in actually implementing the kind of environmental and management controls he feels would be necessary. He thought there would be a conflict between the economic objectives of the Conservative Government and the environmental goals which most of us who have a sense of the environment would like to see achieved.
I believe what we must do in fact is to look at actions when we are considering this whole issue. What actions have been taken? We have been in Government now for 18 months- sometimes it seems a lot shorter and sometimes a lot longer. Let us take, for example, the problem of PCBs. For a long time, possible controls for transportation of PCBs were on the books but were never promulgated. The Government in the spring of last year did that so that there would be rigid controls for the handling and transportation of PCBs. That could have been done a long time before. We have not allowed PCBs as far back as 1978. We had then a pretty full sense of what possible dangers they could lead to, particularly in terms of human health, but it was this Government which brought in this legislation within a period of less than a year from the time of coming to office.
Second, and I think this is a really key point because it also speaks to a point made by the Hon. Member for Cochrane-Superior (Mr. Penner), is the modernization of the pulp and paper industry. Before forming the Government we have had discussions over a period of at least five years concerning acid rain. We did not make as much noise as some members of the Opposition have from time to time. We did not shout and scream. Instead, we reached agreement with every province in Canada concerning our objectives, and then we went into action and put our money where our mouth was. That is the critical difference. Not only did we take action and achieve agreement, we have allocated $150 million to do precisely what the Hon. Member for Cochrane-Superior was suggesting we did not have the political will to do. We put forward that money, to be matched in many cases by the provinces, for the modernization of the smelting industry. I am sure the Hon. Member for Davenport would have liked to have achieved that had he got the co-operation or financial support of his Government when he was the Minister. We did it and it is a major accomplishment.
Along with that, we established automobile emission levels so that in September, 1987, for the 1988 model year, automo-

February 3, 1986
Supply
bile emissions will be reduced by 45 per cent. We can start getting rid of the nitrogen oxide and hydrocarbon and carbon monoxide emissions. Our standards will also result in significant reductions in the amount of lead in the environment, ultimately eliminating it as quickly as possible. Those are specific actions taken in the short time we have been in office. Those actions speak much louder than any words we hear from either of the opposition Parties. It is sometimes difficult in the hue and cry to be fully aware of the real action taken and the positive results achieved in that period of time.
What is hard for me to grasp, Mr. Speaker, is the inconsistency between some of the things the Liberal critic said and what he was able to accomplish. I have heard many excellent words spoken by almost everyone who stood up to speak today on the environment. There can be little debate about the fact that, as the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Epp) said today, the problem of toxic chemicals has been with us since at least the 1940s. It has also been an increasing problem. We hear the Opposition talking about our lack of action, yet when we came into office we walked into a vacuum. As the Hon. Member for Cochrane-Superior indicated-
The vacuum is in your brain.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of the Environment
speechtext: -there were pieces of legislation all over the place which did not accomplish anything. We have a Liberal critic who I guess cannot read. 1 am not sure. They want a statement of will. The interpretation that he chooses to put on some of the things he has raised-

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Liberal Party
speechtext: You are just a bunch of cheap shots. You don't get anything done.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of the Environment
speechtext: If the Hon. Member wants to talk about cheap shots, he should read the speech by the Hon. Member for Davenport.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Liberal Party
speechtext: I was here when he made it. It was a good speech.
Oh, oh!

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of the Environment
speechtext: He may like those cheap shots in the Hon. Member's speech, but I have to tell you that calling the Minister of the Environment names is not a very constructive thing to do if he wants to raise the level of debate.
I didn't call him a name, just described him as Bugs Bunny.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of the Environment
speechtext:
At least 1 have refrained from making some of the obvious comments about the Hon. Member's personality. I think this debate is important enough that it should be at least raised to a higher level.
I would like to read the statement by the Minister which the Hon. Member for Davenport probably has not had an opportunity to read. His concept of what the Environmental Contaminants Act might or might not do is one thing. What the Government intends to do with it is, I think, reflected in the speech by the Minister in Peterborough about one week ago. I
am going to quote directly from that speech and then follow it up with some specific comments to try to give a sense of the constructive actions this Government will be taking. The Minister said this:
The new Act will regulate chemicals from "the cradle to the grave". Specifically, it will prevent the formulation, manufacture, distribution, sale, and use of any new chemical that has not been proven safe, and it will bring order to the system of managing chemicals already in trade and commerce. In cases where accidents occur-and accidents can certainly happen to even the most environmentally sensitive companies-the new law will cover every facet of clean up, including, possibly, compensation to innocent third parties.
The preamble of the new legislation will set out, for all time, the purpose, intention, philosophy, and commitment of the Government of Canada to protect the environment and, thereby, to protect the health and safety of present and future generations alike. The preamble will constitute, in effect if not technically, this country's first "environmental bill of rights".
The Minister went on to say:
The new law will be the strongest of its kind, not only in North America but in the western hemisphere.
I do not think there can be any clearer statement of this Government's intentions, and this will be followed by a specific action.
The Hon. Member for Cochrane-Superior has raised some important points. We have not even had an inventory of the some 65,000 chemicals presently in use in this country and the 1,000 new chemicals which come into the country every year. That has to be done, it is under way, and we will accomplish it. We are one of the few countries in the western industrialized world which does not have that information. This Government has had to live with that fact since coming into office some 18 months ago.
Earlier I spoke of a vacuum. 1 heard some comments about cheap shots and a Member opposite saying that the vacuum was in my head. Let me ask this question. Where was the statement of the Government's environmental policy up until now?

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Liberal Party
speechtext: None.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of the Environment
speechtext:
There was none. There has been none by the Government of Canada until now. That is exactly right. Now this Government has made a statement. 1 would like to ask the Hon. Member for Davenport, if he were still in the House, where is our national water policy? We never had one. It is this Government which will produce a national water policy. Following the federal inquiry on water, in which the Hon. Member for Davenport had some part, we are at a stage where the Cabinet, for the first time, has given responsibility to an individual Minister in this area, and that is the Minister of the Environment. We are looking after our water and all its aspects, including the toxic chemicals therein, including exports, and diversions and all those things. We have that responsibility vested in one Minister, and he will take the responsibility for making sure we have a national water policy which will serve Canadian needs. That is a giant step forward and it helps to Fill the void which has existed for so long.
A lot of issues surrounding toxic chemicals have been raised, certainly in the public's mind if not in this House, by the spill
February 3, 1986

in the St. Clair River. It was an accidental spill but it brought to light some of the problems which have existed for heaven only knows how long. We could not have had a more rapid or specific response to a problem than that by the Minister of the Environment to the difficulties we faced with that spill. Within days we had a full-fledged federal, provincial and industry investigation. The best available facilities were used and federal Government spending has exceeded $1 million, and I assume that the company and the province have spent as much. The situation was followed on a daily basis. There was a competent staff which made a competent clean-up and found out that we were, in fact, dealing not only with a spill, but with a longstanding problem and probably some chronic leakage areas. These things have also been investigated. We received a final report last week, which gives us a framework to look into the future and 24 recommendations which are being acted on by the Government. I do not have time now to delineate all 24 of the recommendations and the specific responses, but this has now been accomplished, Mr. Speaker.
We talk almost blithely about cradle-to-grave management and research. The Government's commitment to research is mentioned frequently. We had many pieces of research on toxics for a long period of time, but it was difficult to know whether we were getting the most effective use of our resources and whether some of the intended expenditures were going to provide the best possible results for the money that would be spent. We had three separate inquiries into toxicology research in Canada; one through the National Research Council, one through Environment Canada, and the final one through the Science Council. All of these have been reported and the Government has taken some specific actions and will take more.
In conjunction with that, I will very quickly mention the toxicology fund. We have supplied seed money of $1 million for a toxicology fund which, under a joint management board, including people from private enterprise, has created a whole series of specific projects. Twenty-one have been submitted to date and, of those, 12 have been accepted. They provide some very interesting and unique approaches into very specific areas of toxicology research. Those things are presently under way. As was mentioned this morning, the Member for Guelph (Mr. Winegard), who is very interested in the possibility of a toxicology centre in that part of the country, is working locally and with Ministers of the Crown to determine whether that type of facility is in fact necessary and appropriate.
To return to the main point, Mr. Speaker, our approach must provide a system that will deal competently and effectively with the issue of toxic chemicals and their potential for getting into our drinking water and affecting our health. It must deal with more than only the St. Clair River, the Niagara River, or a response to a particular spill.
Mention has been made of the IJC. The reaction of the Member for Davenport to the IJC was unfortunate and discouraging for all Members of the House. Be that as it may, the IJC is a specific part of the long-term approach, particularly
Supply
with regard to national boundary waters. The IJC is probably best known to most Canadians for its very constructive and competent work in the 1970s when the Great Lakes, and Lake Erie in particular, faced eutrophication. The amount of difficulty was such that, for all intents and purposes, the lake was dead. I lived in that area and saw what happened to it. The co-operation that was achieved through the International Joint Commission is a real success story. That is the type of activity that we hope to be able to emulate and repeat time and again when it is necessary on matters of this type.
The Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) has filled the two positions which were vacant on the IJC with people who have a level of competence to deal with both political matters and the excellent scientific support staff of the IJC.
Tell us about their backgrounds.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of the Environment
speechtext: The unfortunate thing about the IJC, as the Member for Davenport and anyone who knows anything about it will know, is that during the administration of the last Government that body became almost useless. He doesn't know what the IJC stands for.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of the Environment
speechtext: In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, the Government has the action and the political will. In the future we will produce the results that are necessary to ensure that Canadians have a healthy future and that we manage the toxic chemicals that are an integral part of that future.

Mr. Speaker, could the Parliamentary Secretary clarify why the Government is allowing corn and soy beans to come into Canada from countries that use the chemical ala-chlor known by the trade name of Lasso? On December 31 the Government cancelled the temporary permit which it had allowed for this herbicide since last February. Farmers in southwestern Ontario who depend on this for use in the production of their crops are wondering why, if this chemical is being cancelled for use in Canada, corn and soy beans from the United States, where its use is allowed, are being allowed into Canada. Can the Parliamentary Secretary assure us that countries which use this chemical will not be allowed to ship corn and soy beans into Canada?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of the Environment
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Hon. Member for Algoma (Mr. Foster) has given us another example of Government action in an area where there had previosuly been inaction. My understanding is that we have, in fact, cancelled the use of alachlor in Canada. My understanding, subject to confirmation, is also that there is no residue left by the product. 1 am not positive of that and I will say that very clearly so that I do not intentionally mislead him. However, my understanding is that there is no residue left by the product. If that is the case, it poses no threat to our health through getting into to ecosystem in any way. Even if that is not the case, I under-

With regard to the appointees to the IJC, I had the privilege of meeting today with Mr. Bob Welch, a very distinguished person from the Niagara Peninsula in Ontario who has knowledge and a grasp of some of the problems of the environment in the peninsula. I am glad that the Parliamentary Secretary mentioned that. The Member also mentioned that this is a Government of action regarding acid rain. The agreements which the Government has now made with the provinces and the expenditure of SI50 million certainly let the people of Canada know that the Government is going to deal with this issue, and also the Bill of Rights to which the Parliamentary Secretary alluded.
During the 1980 election the then Prime Minister, Mr. Trudeau, journeyed to the Niagara Peninsula and came to Niagara Falls. The cleaning up of the Niagara River, Love Canal and Hooker Chemical with all the sludge pouring into the lower Niagara River was a major election issue at that time. The Prime Minister made some amazing statements, such as that this would be at the forefront of his Government's concern about the environment.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of the Environment
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker the inability of the former Government to accomplish anything is unfortunate. I understand that its intentions were often good, especially on the part of the Member for Davenport, but he was unable to accomplish anything.
I expect him to criticize the Government in our efforts to resolve some of these outstanding problems. However, the first step in being able to resolve these problems is to establish a level of communication and confidence. I recognize that it may not be a perfect first step.
Opposition Members have said that we are wasting time because it is the fault of the Americans that we have been unable to achieve a bilateral agreement on acid rain. However, such an agreement requires two parties, and the relative inability of the former Government to put this issue on the agenda with the Americans at the presidential and prime ministerial level speaks volumes in terms of the relationship.
We have established a working relationship and while we have our separate points of view, and hope to have the Americans understand and accept our view, this may not be accomplished immediately. However, we are on the right track and that is the great difference with what we have seen before.

Mr. Speaker, I hope the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of the Environment (Mr. Gurbin) can assure us that Government will put controls on the importation of corn from those states which permit the use of alachlor in its production. Such controls are also important with respect to the use of alachlor in the production of soya beans because it obviously puts our farmers at a disadvantage in the production of that crop. I assume he will discuss this with the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Wise) to ensure that corn produced with that chemical in the United States will not be allowed into Canada.
The Hon. Member talked about the Guelph Toxicology Centre. He said that the Member for Guelph (Mr. Winegard) is reviewing the feasibility of that project with the Minister and other officials. That project was ready to proceed. It had the staff and was under construction over a year ago, on November 8, when it was cancelled by the Government. If it really wanted it to proceed it would not have cancelled that project. There was a $16 million commitment by the federal and provincial Governments and another $8 million from the private sector. It should have proceeded.
That project was moving ahead when the Hon. Member for Davenport (Mr. Caccia) was the Minister of the Environment. It was a model project in a field in which we need a toxicology centre of excellence for training and research. We have seen over a year lost on a project that is essential to the environment and toxicology research, and I hope the Government will reinstate it immediately.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of the Environment
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we must take two factors into consideration when discussing a toxicology centre and toxicology research in Canada. First, we must consider how a toxicology centre will be run and on what basis. Second, there is the financial factor.
Let me give the Hon. Member a specific example. Toxicology research in Canada was taking place on a year-by-year basis. A number of the projects which were claimed to be cancelled were, in fact, completed. There was no long-term funding. That is precisely why the three groups from the National Research Council, Environment Canada and the Science Council were mandated, either by themselves or in cooperation with the Government, to determine what type of long-term toxicology research should take place.
We must also consider the operating costs of those establishments in addition to the capital expenditure. This is where fiscal responsibility must be taken into account, and 1 know that whatever determination is made for that facility, if it occurs, it will achieve concrete goals in the long-term best interests of this question.

Mr. Speaker, the Hon. Parliamentary Secretary dealt with the theme of action and political will. He gave
February 3, 1986

a number of excellent examples of the demonstration of political will and action on the part of the Government which have been seen already. However, the Parliamentary Secretary is aware that there are some questions among the public as to the Government's will to proceed with some of these particular items, even though they have been announced.
Are the rumours about the postponement of the automobile emission standards correct? Second, as far as the amendments to the Environmental Contaminants Act are concerned, has the Government made a firm commitment to proceed with those amendments and, if so, when will we see them introduced in the House?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of the Environment
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as far as the automobile emissions are concerned, unfortunately, The Toronto Star editorial which dealt with this subject raised some unnecessary questions. If the research had been better, they would understand that the Government has not backed down. The controls were always meant to be effective for the 1988 models to be introduced in September, 1987.
We realized that some 1987 models would still be in production after September. The only change is to indicate that all 1988 models, as originally intended, will be affected. We will not impose these controls on companies finishing their 1987 model runs.
I believe it is general knowledge that automobile companies usually change their model runs in September. Rather than backing down, we have listened to the realistic proposals of the companies to let them finish their 1987 models production.
The Hon. Member asked about the Environmental Contaminants Act. We have a specific agenda and program for Cabinet submission. I do not want to give the Hon. Member a firm date for introduction to the House, but we do have a proposal and I hope we will be able to follow through with it. I think he will be happy with the time frame.

The House resumed consideration of the motion of Mr. Caccia:
That this House condemns the Government for its failure to recognize the importance attributed by Canadians to toxic chemicals in water and other elements of the environment.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the spokesman on the environment for the Official Opposition has moved:
That this House condemns the Government for its failure to recognize the importance attributed by Canadians to toxic chemicals in water and other elements of the environment.
This is an important and timely motion. All one has to do to confirm this is to look at the report which was published only last December by a special committee to review the Great Lakes Water Quality Agreements, of the Royal Society of Canada and the National Research Council of the United States of America. That report, speaking about the water quality of the Great Lakes, said that "toxic contaminants represented the greatest immediate threat to the interests of future generations". Unfortunately they represent a serious threat to the present generation as well. The fact is that when it comes to toxic chemicals in our environment, we are facing a serious situation, one that is potentially even more serious if urgent action is not taken right now.
Earlier today the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Epp), speaking on behalf of the Government, tried to say that the Government has recognized the problem and its priority. To see if this is correct, let us look at the record just in connection with the problem of toxic chemicals in the St. Clair River. If we look at that situation, we see that in September, 1985, test results were released showing that what is now known as the toxic chemical blob on the bottom of the St. Clair River contained, among other dangerous chemicals, dioxin, one of the most toxic chemicals known to mankind. The fact of the matter is that the sample which provided these test results was taken more than a year before, in August, 1984. That sample was taken by divers working for the Great Lakes Institute of the University of Windsor, funded by a program provided by the previous Liberal Government. The Minister has never explained, at least not in any satisfactory way, why his Department sat on that sample for more than a year without completing the test results showing the dangerous toxic chemical situation connected with the toxic blob on the bottom of the St. Clair River. He has never explained why that sample was not tested immediately or why the action about which he talked in respect of setting up the joint task force of the federal and provincial Governments was not taken a year earlier, immediately after the sample was originally taken by

divers working for the Great Lakes Institute of the University of Windsor.
Let us be clear about the situation we are describing. As I have said, dioxin is considered to be one of the most dangerous chemicals known to mankind. Last week it was disclosed that tests taken only recently showed traces of dioxin in the drinking water of Windsor and three other communities downstream from the St. Clair River. The federal Minister of the Environment (Mr. McMillan) said that the amounts found in these tests were minute and below acceptable levels for safety. I will say more about that in a minute, but 1 repeat again that the Minister has never explained the delay in completing the tests on the sample taken in August, 1984 by the divers working for the Great Lakes Institute of the University of Windsor.
Let us be clear. When we are talking about acceptable standards for dioxin, the evidence is that the standard about which we are talking is a temporary standard, one set only in the last week or so. It is an interim standard, which means that it is one capable of being adjusted downward in the light of further research and further evidence. We are not talking about a standard which is the result of final conclusions by experts working in the field of toxic chemicals. In fact, what is disturbing about all this is that the United States Environmental Protection Agency indicated that there was no safe level for dioxins. Yet, the federal Minister of the Environment tries to tell us that there is nothing to worry about. He made a statement based upon what he admitted was only an interim or temporary standard, one capable of adjustment in the future. Perhaps the adjustment will be upward, but also, unfortunately, it could be downward.
It seems that if we are to take seriously what the Minister of National Health and Welfare said today and what the Minister of the Environment has said on other occasions about their desire to deal with the problem of toxic chemicals in the St. Clair River and toxic chemicals in our environment generally, I think there has to be a greater recognition than can be found in the Ministers' words so far that the situation is serious. We on all sides of the House, on behalf of millions of Canadians and their families and future generations, must insist that immediate action be taken by federal and provincial Governments to deal with the problem of toxic chemicals in the St. Clair River and generally in our environment, and what it means for people in downriver communities such as my own City of Windsor. There must be a commitment to action, a definite plan and a definite timetable for taking and implementing the action in question. We have not seen this as yet.
When I speak of the need for commitment by the federal Minister of the Environment and the federal Government, I say that to show that commitment the Minister must stop his practice of casting aside, downgrading publicly in the House, any of his own experts who raise concerns beyond those he is willing to recognize at the time those concerns are expressed. The House will remember how, in response to a question from myself, the Minister rejected and cast aside Darryl Cowell, one of his officials, who told the press that the leakage of toxic
chemical wastes in the St. Clair River could create the biggest hazardous waste problem in North America. We now see from the report of the joint federal-provincial task force which looked into the situation in the St. Clair River that we cannot at all exclude the possibility that toxic chemicals are leaking into the river from dump sites or wells used for the storage of toxic chemicals. That report leaves that question very much open and calls for further detailed studies into the whole matter of possible leakage of toxic chemicals into the St. Clair River. Therefore, when the official of the Minister's Department, Mr. Cowell, pointed out the possibility that it could be the source of a great ecological disaster, the last thing the Minister should have done was to reject and rebuke publicly the official in question.
The Minister should not have done the same thing to Dr. Hallett of his Department when Dr. Hallett released disturbing findings about the levels of PCBs in the food we eat. When I raised that question in the House, the Minister said that Dr. Hallett was speaking at a seminar and, since it was not organized by his Department, it did not represent something which could be given credence and weight by his Department. I do not think it should have made any difference where Dr. Hallett made his remarks, provided they were worthy of attention and support. There seems to be confirmation of Doctor Hallett's concerns in the report of the Royal Society of Canada and the National Research Council of the United States, which I referred to earlier. I personally do not think it was completely a coincidence that Doctor Hallett chose to leave the Department shortly after he was publicly disavowed in this House by the Minister of the Environment. Certainly the Minister has not been creating in his Department a congenial atmosphere for experts who dare to challenge the Minister's own conventional knowledge on the subject. Also, as I have said previously, people like Doctor Hallett, I would think, know a lot more about the problem than does the Minister.
In addition to real commitment by the Minister and his Government, more commitment than has been shown until now, there has to be a meaningful plan of action. That plan must involve steps to be taken right now. So far the Minister's only answer is to say that at some vague, unspecified future date the Minister will be presenting legislation to this House to update the Environmental Contaminants Act. Well, surely that is not the answer, or at least it is only a very small part of the answer.
The report of the special task force of federal and provincial officials on the St. Clair River shows how much more has to be done. That report contains 24 specific and pointed recommendations. What concerns me, and I am sure it concerns the people of my community of Windsor and the people of the entire Great Lakes region, is that at no time in this debate today did the Government state clearly and specifically that it would accept and act on those 24 recommendations as a matter of urgency. Surely this is a minimum requirement to expect from this Government if it is to be taken seriously when
February 3, 1986

it says it has a real commitment to taking action on toxic chemicals in the St. Clair River, in the Great Lakes, and in our environment generally.
This report shows that the industries are discharging into the St. Clair River higher levels of toxic chemicals than existing standards permit. The report also says that there are many toxic chemicals which are being discharged by companies into the St. Clair River for which standards do not yet exist. Surely immediate action should be taken on this. Certainly because of the lack of absolute certainty about what are safe standards for dioxin in drinking water, if they exist at all, the federal Government must act now, together with the provinces, to help municipalities like Windsor to have special filtration systems installed to remove dioxin from its drinking water, no matter how small the traces. The Minister certainly should not have rejected, as he did in the House, the utility of activated charcoal systems as an urgent response to the findings of dioxin in the drinking water of Windsor and three other area communities.
It is interesting that while the Minister says that activated charcoal filtration systems do not have to be made available to communities like Windsor at this time, only last week the Ontario Minister of the Environment was willing to say that he is working on setting up and installing, at the very least, some special experimental filtration systems in the area. I would strongly urge the Minister to consider the community of Windsor as one of the ideal and logical places for such a system.
I say that the burden of protecting Canadians from toxic chemicals in the water they drink should not have to fall primarily on the municipalities and municipal taxpayers. Surely, the real priority must be on stopping the discharge, the dumping of toxic chemicals by industry into the St. Clair River and other waterways. Our ultimate objective has to be zero discharge of contaminants by industry. Our real priority must be to stop these toxic chemicals from being discharged into our lakes and rivers. Governments must ensure that Firms are in a position to have up-to-date equipment to ensure that there are no accidental spills. Governments might take steps to ensure that the amount of toxic chemicals that is above agreed on standards is not allowed to be dumped through sewer systems into our lakes and rivers.
Surely, Mr. Speaker, there are steps the federal Government can and must take now, steps of the kind outlined by the Hon. Member for Davenport (Mr. Caccia). The Government could reinstate the two-year accelerated write-offs under the Income Tax Act as an incentive to industry to get modern treatment equipment in place, to separate sewers, to put in modern monitoring systems, and to ensure that the highest standards of waste treatment are applied. This must be a step taken to buttress having in place an adequate and up-to-date system of control regulation. This is one of the key recommendations of the special task force of officials, federal and provincial, on the St. Clair River problem. They make clear that we do not have an adequate system of control regulation in place now, and this has to be an urgent priority. We must, as the report says:

-develop control regulation for the industries and municipalities discharging to the St. Clair River. Through this control regulation, the Ministry of the Environment, with the scientific and technical support of the DOE, will establish effluent concentrations and loading levels for all parameters which, if exceeded, will trigger additional monitoring, remedial measures, abatement and prosecution.
The federal Government could well offer a special program for municipalities like Sarnia and Windsor and provide financial assistance for the installation of equipment facilities for the best possible treatment of residential, commercial and industrial waste waters that pass through municipal sewer systems. Also, as pointed out by the Hon. Member for Davenport and as I pointed out in the House last fall, the federal Government could create a super fund with interested provincial Governments to remove toxic waste from dumps, and therefore remove the source of future problems at leaking dumps. As I have said, this is something I called for in the House last fall, months ago, and at that time the Minister said he was interested in working to set up a super fund with the Province of Ontario. So far I have seen no progress by the Minister to carry out and put into reality the expression of interest he put forward in response to my question to the House last fall. This is something which has to be a priority of the Minister if we are to take him seriously and if we are to take the Government seriously.
We have to act now. We should not have to ask Canadians to even consider trade-offs between jobs in industries like those along the St. Clair River and their health and safety and the health and safety of their families and of the communities in which they live. The manufacturing and the installation of appropriate control technology is itself a form of job creating economic activity. The costs of control of toxic chemicals over time are surely less than the costs of the destruction of our environment, of our forests, of our waters, and of the loss of health of millions of Canadians through excess ingestion of toxic chemicals.
The report of the National Research Council and of the Canadian Royal Society points out the economical benefits of damage avoided, but it also deals with the terrible consequences of not dealing with toxic chemicals and the pollution they create right now. I raised this matter in the House on a number of occasions in the past and I am pleased to raise it in the House today to join in the cry for action by my colleagues in the Official Opposition, and hopefully other Members as well. I am speaking out for my constituents and my community, but also I am speaking out for all Canadians. We need more than the pious but unfortunately all too empty words of the Government and its representatives. So far we have seen nothing more. That is not enough for the people of my community and the people of Canada. Let us have action. Without that action, the Government stands justly condemned by present and future generations.
