Mr. Speaker, I am glad to be able to participate in this debate, particularly because the motion before us was moved by a former Minister of the Environment, the Hon. Member for Davenport (Mr. Caccia), the constituency in which 1 had the great pleasure to grow up. Those were happier days when Davenport was a Conservative riding.
Hear, hear!

Nonetheless, I am happy that the attention of the House today is focused upon the subject before us. There are few concerns of the Canadian people more vital than the concern for the environment. I welcome the Hon. Member's motion. However, when 1 read it, I have to think that the motion itself borders on the hypocritical. It condemns the Government for ignoring the concerns of the people with respect to the development of their environment. It ignores the types of constant achievement to which reference has been made and which should be reiterated. The Government has taken many steps in this regard.
For example, it found some $300 million to help cut sulphur dioxide emissions in half by the year 1994. It has imposed more stringent emission standards for motor vehicles, cars and trucks, which will cut hydrocarbons by 80 per cent and which will bring about significant reductions in the emissions of carbon monoxide, nitrogen oxides and evaporative emissions. All of this will contribute significantly to the well-being of the environment and its impact upon our water supply. These are steps which have been taken. These are actions which have been declared and which are to take effect in the near future. The Government has also imposed stricter requirements for the transportation of PCBs.
I regret the wording of the motion. Not only does it ignore the positive actions which have been taken by the Government, it ignores the reality that we have a problem now. We have a problem now for two reasons. The first reason is the limited action which the previous Government and the previous Minister of the Environment took, something which is not recognized at all in the motion or in the presentations of Hon. Members thus far. Second, it ignores the reality that there is

no quick fix available to anyone regardless of what Party is in office and regardless of who is the Minister. This is a problem of such enormormity and complexity that we are simply never going to have an immediate solution. However, we must take seriously the challenge and work progressively step by step and consistently toward keeping it under control and improving our environment.
If we look to some of the reports which are available to us, we will find one report entitled Time Lost, A Demand for Action on Acid Rain. This is a report put out by the Subcommittee on Acid Rain which was appointed during the years of the previous Government. On page 3 of that report we find a reference to the report of a previous committee of the House submitted in October of 1981 entitled Still Waters, which included 38 recommendations. Were they all enacted? Did they all become operative? Did they all transform the environment?
One reason for the debate today is that those 38 recommendations did not become fully part of the policies of the Government of the day. Thus, we find the committee of 1981 not having the satisfaction of seeing all its recommendations being put into effect. We find that its successor committee- there was need for another committee just a few years later- stated that the situation is so serious that:
-Canadians, including members of this Sub-committee, who have travelled to the United States to argue for more stringent controls on American polluters, Canadian government inaction and/or obstinacy with respect to domestic controls have been, quite frankly, an embarrasment.
That is how a committee of the House, with a majority of members from the Government of the day, reacted to the Government of which the Hon. Member who moved the motion and the Hon. Member who just gave his address were members. In the view of the committee the lack of inaction and the obstinacy of the previous Government was a cause of embarrasment. These were not simply critics from outside the House or members of the Opposition but Members who supported the Government.
I would like to turn to page 12 of the same report under the heading "Emission Control Standards". On that page there is a reference made to two recommendations which were put into the hands of the Government and of the Minister. It states:
Neither of these recommendations has been adopted by the Federal Government.
On page 13 it states:
The present Canadian regulatory position is therefore an enomaly, is environmentally harmful, and causes acute political embarrasment to Canadians in discussions with U.S. legislators and officials on the need for continental controls on acid rain.
That is the record of the previous Government and the several Ministers of the Environment which it appointed. That is the result-the embarrasment of Canadians generally in negotiating environmental policies with our neighbour to the south.
The report continues on page 41:
Clearly, the attack on acid rain, if it is to be successful, must be a joint Canada-United States effort. Unfortunately, the political will needed to tackle the problem is lacking in the United States.
That is a recognition of reality. We cannot solve the problem on our own, regardless of what Party forms the Government or what Member is the Minister. We need the co-operation of a neighbour with whom we must negotiate. There is no power that we have available to us by which we can compel them to act. We must pursue, as our predecessors did, a process of negotiation, anticipating in negotiation that we can persuade by information, by agreement and by bargaining that some action will be taken. However, let us recognize that if we are to have any sense of reality in the House of Commons at all, then there is no Government that can simply act unilaterally. No Government can simply take action which will not require the agreement of the United States if we are to deal adequately with the problem. So I have to ask why the Official Opposition Party affronts this House of Commons and the rationality of the Canadian people by condemning the Government for not making the environment a perfect situation which this resolution implies is within the scope of the Government, when that Party, having been 20 years in office, found itself incapable of achieving that kind of perfection.
I feel that anyone on this side of the House would border on the irrational if he or she were to say to the Opposition: "Well, you should have made it perfect. You should have achieved an environment in which there would not be a single pollutant in existence". We must have some common sense sometimes, and let us show it by recognizing the achievements which have become part of the Canadian scene in the past 15 months. We should respect as well those achievements which I gladly recognize as part of the record of the previous Government. But we must recognize that there are challenges we must take seriously and work hard at if we are going to carry forward that which we have begun since September, 1984.
Let me point out two difficulties which must be kept in mind in dealing with the environment. First, there is a sociological challenge, which receives all too little recognition in a debate such as we are having today. For this I cite the former United States Ambassador to Canada, the Honourable Adolph W. Schmidt. In addressing the Empire Club of Canada as far back as 1970, he pointed out the significance of two sociological developments. The first was unrestricted population growth which, we could add, escalated rapidly, which put a pressure upon the environmental outlets required for human existence. Coupled with that problem is the challenge of the congestion of population centres. Mr. Schmidt projected then that it was foreseeable that in a short time 90 per cent of the population of the United States would be living in Five urban regions. Just conceive, Mr. Speaker, the pressure that would put upon the environment surrounding those regions.
Faced with the kind of population development we are experiencing on both sides of the border, and faced with the congestion of urban population, let us recognize that, yes, here
February 3, 1986

is a challenge we have to face, a challenge which must be given a priority over and over again year by year. Let us not be so foolhardy as to believe or imply that some Government is just going to wave a magic legislative or budgetary wand and put an end to pollution.
Let us also face the reality of the political challenge. I quote from a short article in the New York Times which was authored by Charles Phelps which points out that the eight top polluting industries, sources of high sulphur coal, are in states with major deposits of that coal. These eight states hold 105 votes in the House of Representatives, which takes them half way to a majority in that chamber. In contrast, three quarters of the low sulphur coal in the United States is in three states with only six votes in the House of Representatives. That means that when we endeavour to negotiate a correction to the acid rain situation, which affects us all so significantly in Canada, we are up against a major political challenge. There is no way in which we can resolve that challenge and overcome it in the short term and by some magic that we, or another Party in this Chamber, might possess. Let us recognize the foolishness of thinking that we in Ottawa or those in Washington are going to solve it as if sweet reason were enough. We are dealing with a political reality. We have to keep pressing as did our Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) in seeing that it was on the agenda of the Quebec Summit and as he did in seeing that there was a top level commission appointed to report to the President and the Prime Minister. It was composed of such distinguished Canadian citizens as the former Premier of Ontario, the Honourable William Davis. My reason for referring to that is simply to indicate that the kind of progress we are enjoying under this Government and the kind of progress we achieved under the previous Government is expressive of reality. There is no revolutionary solution. We must expect that evolution will be the way we will follow. We will have to move step by step towards achieving the kind of environment we could wish for ourselves and for those who come after.
However, let us not ignore the positive results which that process has achieved. For example, in another study report to which I will refer called Water is a Mainstream Issue, an interim report of an inquiry on federal water supply which was appointed by the previous Government, there is a reference to the kind of progress we have enjoyed by working together and seeking co-operation from the provincial Governments as well as Governments of certain States of the Union and the American Government itself. We should not ignore the kind of achievement to which this report refers, and I quote:
Notable progress has been made with point sources, such as effluent flow from major industries like pulp and paper and petroleum refining, and from municipal sewage treatment plants.
The report does not ignore the lack of progress in other areas and in other connections, and we should not ignore it. But let us remember and recognize that certain things are being achieved and certain progress is being made. The report goes on to ask a question which this House should not ignore and which the report does not answer. It is this:

Can governmental controls catch up with the number and variety of pollutants? Do we need control of chemicals from creation to disposal, as urged by many environmentalists?
If the answer is yes, then certainly that answer is not going to receive quick actualization by any government that will command a majority in this House. It is going to have to be a matter of steady, gradual, but not slow, progress, and to that end this Government is clearly committed.
We should also recognize the wisdom of the International Joint Commission which states in its most recent report:
Significant achievements have been recorded in controlling certain types and sources of pollution, particularly in the areas of point source control of phosphorus and in the control of a number of other conventional pollutants.
That report was dated December 31, 1984. I think very seriously about the condition of the lake on which my city borders, and where I have spent all of my life. I have seen the lake lose the kind of purity which it enjoyed in my boyhood. I recognize the progress which has been achieved by both federal and provincial Governments of both Parties in each instance, and I would like to take a moment to draw to the attention of the House that one great day each year which shows what can happen when there is environmental action taken. That is the annual salmon hunt sponsored by the Toronto Star. A large supply of salmon was put into Lake Ontario to see, first, if the lake could provide a life-giving environment again, and to see as well if a lampreycide was effective. In 1979 each salmon caught in that great tournament showed the marks of lamprey upon it, each one. However, in 1985 only one in 75 caught had those marks. I cite that not to say we are doing wonders, let us rest on our laurels and be proud of our record. I say it to point out how positive accomplishments can be achieved. We must keep working at this cause. A solution is possible, but it is not going to be done tomorrow morning. We have to keep working at it. The only way to do that is by steady, progressive action.
I want to close my remarks by simply saying this. One of the great political leaders of this country was the Hon. Tommy Douglas. I had a great affection and respect for him. He was in this House when I first arrived here. He used to close almost every speech with these words: "I shall not sleep, nor shall my sword stay idle in my hands, till we have built Jerusalem in this green and pleasant land". He spoke those words so frequently that one might have thought they were part of the Regina Manifesto. Actually they were written by the English poet William Blake. He was referring not to the prospect of socialism but to the horror of the impact of the Industrial Revolution upon rural England. Hear, hear!

Minister of the Environment (Mr. McMillan) made cuts in the environmental program it was to do away with duplication. There were no cuts of anything that is vital at this time. I add as well that it is an indication of the Government's interest in the subject of research in the environment that the needs of the Guelph research centre as a centre that can serve the well-being of Canada are undergoing reassessment. In this instance, as in so many, the Government is doing all that it can with the finances available to it. When we face the reality that most of the income tax revenue received by the Government is going to pay off interest on the debt, we see that there is very little surplus left for anything else.
Mr. Speaker, if we can escape from some of the partisan gibes which are going back and forth, I think that this particular issue-
The NDP is totally non-partisan.

Not when it comes to the Member for Hamilton East (Ms. Copps) I fear, but on issues we try to be. We have in front of us an immense challenge which, frankly, is a challenge at which the previous Government failed, and which the present Government, to its credit, is attempting to confront. The Minister has, I think, shown some concern and enthusiasm and, frankly, some very healthy skepticism with respect to the claims of industry with regard to the issue of toxic pollution of our waterways.
The challenge is extremely great and I must ask, at the start of a speech like this, whether it is a challenge that it is possible for this Minister ultimately to meet successfully. Basically what we as a people and a country are doing is using our earth and our surroundings as a garbage can. We are using it for garbage which is perhaps the most dangerous, hazardous and vicious that this planet has ever had to confront. We have to
Supply
change our approach if we are going to succeed in creating a future for the generations that will come after us.
I think the challenge is particularly difficult for three reasons, Mr. Speaker. First, we have a scientific challenge which is very, very complicated. We can learn from this scientific challenge by looking at occupational health as an issue. We have discovered, for instance, that people who used asbestos to produce essential items during wartime found that the asbestos that they worked with, without thinking that it was dangerous, was in fact a time bomb. That time bomb did not hit days later, weeks later, or months later, but years later. Often that time bomb did not hit because of large amounts of asbestos, but because of extremely minute particles of that material which, in a cumulative way, over time, led to people developing the most horrendous possible diseases which debilitated them.
There has not been a single study done on the octadioxin which has just been identified in the drinking water of my community of Windsor, to determine its long-run, cumulative effect on people who imbibe it in a long-run, cumulative way.
Second, there is a lack of knowledge which, fortunately, we are starting to do something about. As an example of that lack of knowledge, Mr. Speaker, out of the 58 chemicals that make up the infamous blob in the St. Clair River, only three have standards which tell us how much can get into fish before those fish are dangerous to people. That lack of knowledge can only be seen as incredibly dangerous to the people who fish in Lake St. Clair in my constituency.
We have a challenge too, Mr. Speaker, to recognize that we as a country are committed to economic development and that our people have come to expect it. Yet, that economic development must recognize the environment as a central concern or else it is not an economic development that is counting the costs of economic growth. Those are intellectual and political challenges that are very, very tough for any Government, whether Conservative, Liberal, or Socialist. Those are very difficult intellectural challenges to face. Above all, however, they are challenges that must be faced with urgency and a passionate commitment to do something about them. Unfortunately, it is not yet possible to detect such action on the part of the Government.
Let me take Members of the House through the recent happenings on the St. Clair River. It is a drama which in fact turned out to be far more interesting, explosive and powerful to this country than the divers who first brought up the dioxin-laden globs in 1984 which set this struggle off first thought. In fact, it was one of those divers who came to my office a year after those tests were first conducted in 1984 and said that they discovered something but still have not heard from the various ministries, including Liberal and Conservative ministries, what that dangerous chemical was.
We began to ask questions about that discovery, what it was and how dangerous. It was only as those questions began to be asked in September, 1985-a year after those tests had been conducted-that the Ministries decided to begin retesting. It

was then that they discovered that indeed the great toxic blob had in fact not disappeared but, even worse, was now present in concentrations twice as high as had been true when it was discovered in 1984. Furthermore, it was not the easy form of octadioxin that the Minister talked about but the much more dangerous toxic and hazardous forms of tetradioxin, in heavier concentrations than had been true in 1984.
Yet, a whole year had passed without any action being taken to clean up that disaster. Finally, after a second test was conducted which showed these dangerous concentrations and after pushing and prodding, the federal Minister and Ontario Minister finally took action and a joint study was conducted. That joint study, unlike virtually any other study I have seen, did not come up with a set of conclusions. It came up with a set of questions. I strongly suggest to Members of the House that they read through the recommendations of this recent report on St. Clair River pollution investigations. They will find repeatedly that the recommendations do not give an answer to what needs to be done but recommend what should be investigated further. It states, for example, that we must investigate the Michigan site and the source of the dioxins and furons.
In short, the report in itself if not an answer but an action plan to find an answer. That is why the crucial question that faces the Government right now is what it will do about the 24 recommendations in this report. If it can tell the House of Commons today that it will follow up on every single recommendation as urgently, fully and comprehensively as necessary to find the answer, it will finally have taken the first step toward convincing those who care about the environment that it actually has that sense of urgency and commitment.
I want to talk briefly about the politics of this issue. Frankly, I have found it to be a political learning experience. It has been exciting to use information, sometimes gathered from unorthodox sources, and to pose questions effectively so that the Government will move to take an issue seriously, as I believe it has done with respect to the St. Clair River issue. My colleague says that the Government needed that kick in the butt to get at this concern.
However, there is another part of the politics of this issue that has also been fascinating, that is, to see the Conservative Members of Parliament who represent the areas which are sources of this pollution try to defend their localities. Surely it is possible, as indeed the Deputy Prime Minister (Mr. Nielsen) did today, for people to get up in the House and admit past mistakes. Surely it is possible for communities or companies to admit that they have not given the proper attention to pollution control.
Why was it necessary that the politics of this issue had to be raised by those Members who represent constituencies downriver from this pollution spill? It should have been Members of Parliament from the spill areas themselves who pushed this issue. Perhaps it is the nature of politics in our society that it is up to us in our communities downriver from these pollution crises to make the issue come alive and give it the drama which brings the attention that, in turn, builds the focus of
Government on the issue as a crucial question which must be dealt with and corrected.
We have a new report. It is a report which carries with it the urgency of this issue. It is a report which tells us in the communities downriver from the St. Clair that we can expect some reassurance from the Government that it will take our problems seriously. It is a report which must be acted upon. I ask the Government, the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) and the Ministers responsible to take this report with the seriousness that it deserves. I ask them to see to it, in respect of the 24 recommendations in the report, that the possibility of underground sources of pollution is probed completely, and to see to it that the problems of fish in Lake St. Clair are studied as they deserve to be studied for the people of my constituency. Also I ask them to see to it that a year from today, instead of three of the 58 chemicals having standards for fish quality, all 58 have full standards for fish quality and for water quality, and that we have a sense of the cumulative impact of these different chemicals mixing together.
I should like to refer to our fight in Windsor. The Clean Water Alliance has been formed and met yesterday with 300 people to raise concerns about this issue. It is not only a fight for our selfish interests in the St. Clair River basin. It is a fight for change across the country to make pollution the urgent issue which it has to be. As our environment critic, the Hon. Member for Winnipeg-Brids Hill (Mr. Blaikie), has made clear, it is a fight for a safe drinking water Act, for an environmental bill of rights, for speedy introduction of tough amendments to the Environmental Contaminants Act, and for a tough Canadian response to the refusal of the Environmental Protection Agency so far to act in the Niagara situation.
We must stop using our earth and our environment as a garbage can. We must, on a non-partisan basis throughout the House, make a commitment to our future and the future of our children. We must make this issue have the urgency it deserves as we head toward the end of the 20th century and the beginning of the 21st century.

Member, despite his compliments, that the way to progress is to cut back some of our research centres. speechtext: Unfortunately, there is no more time.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to begin by congratulating the Hon. Member for Davenport (Mr. Caccia) for introducing into the public forum an issue which is obviously of concern to every Canadian. That issue is specifically not only the particular problems which have been identified and are being examined in the St. Clair River, but also the general question of water quality and the concerns surrounding the level of toxic chemicals which are being found not only in the St. Clair River but also in other major bodies of water. As a Member of Parliament for Hamilton East I have in my riding an area known as the Windermere basin, which has been identified by the International Joint Commission as one of the most polluted bodies of water in North America. Naturally when we read daily accounts in the media about the difficulty facing the people in the St. Clair River area and those people who are concerned about their drinking water, we too, in the frontier of Lake Ontario have to be concerned in the same way because I think that there is a general feeling among the public that the whole story has yet to be revealed.
In fact, there are a lot of questions, and I have constituents who call my office and say, "Is the water safe to drink? We have seen in the City of Toronto on a number of occasions the beaches being closed and, in fact, even the water itself being examined for levels of toxicity which are absolutely unacceptable. I am sorry to say that even in my own community there is not a regular, systematic review done to measure the level of
dioxin toxicity in the drinking water. It happens to be a piecemeal operation which does not address the very serious concerns which have forced many constituents into the private market to buy their water.
I would respectfully differ with the position of the Hon. Member for Guelph (Mr. Winegard) who has suggested that somehow we will solve this problem by turning over our research capacity to the private sector. It is pretty clear that the private sector will have to concern itself first and foremost with the bottom line and with more immediate results. One of the benefits which had been derived from programs like the herring-gull program, which was snuffed out by this Government, and snuffed out not only by the Minister of the Environment (Mr. McMillan) but aided and abetted by the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. de Cotret), and the slasher himself, the Deputy Prime Minister (Mr. Nielsen).
This particular program was prepared to take a long-term look and to develop the kind of data base necessary to attack the problem in Lake Ontario which services the drinking water of more than three million people in its direct vicinity. Instead, in a penny ante approach to long-term environmental solutions, the Minister decided to cut off that program and to say that even though we were seeing deformities being identified in herring gull eggs we were not prepared to carry on with this program because it did not meet the Deputy Prime Minister's bottom line, even though at the time that same Conservative Government promised that the environmental project and the research would not be cut.
We know, Mr. Speaker, that that is simply not the case. We also know, with the cut-backs and the decision by the Government of Canada not to fund to Guelph Toxicology Centre, that the Government is abdicating its responsibility to the private sector suggesting that the private sector will be there to pick up the pieces. The private sector has some immediate shortterm concerns relating to productivity and the bottom line. The private sector is not prepared to look at an over-all question of water quality, for example, in the area of the Great Lakes.
Let us take a look at the question of food production and how toxic chemicals impinge upon the food production on a daily basis. We have seen more and more reports about irradiation and what is being allowed to be done to preserve the shelf life of our food in a way that could be extremely detrimental to the health of every Canadian.
I would suggest that private companies in the business of food production will not hold back on irradiation because the long term effects of that process may not be known for many years. We have a responsibility in government to provide leadership in these most difficult areas. I say they are difficult because they involve co-operation at the federal, provincial and municipal levels.
I heard Members on the government side of the House citing, chapter and verse, the shortcomings of the previous Liberal Government with respect to its environmental policy. I
February 3, 1986

would like to point out that one of the first and most effective actions of the new Liberal Government in Ontario has been to introduce a spills Bill which, for the first time, will allow companies, unions, workers and the public to have a handle on just what kind of toxic chemicals are being dealt with in industry across Ontario, information which was not only kept secret by the previous Conservative Government, but over which it chose to distribute its own products, its own toxic wines in our liquor stores.
The Liberal Government in Ontario has made it a number one priority not only to introduce the spills Bill but to act on legislation originally recommended by the then Leader of the Liberal Party, now Chairman of the Science Council, Stuart Smith. The Liberal Party has been on the record on this issue in Ontario for many years and finally has had an opportunity to put forth legislation which will make a change in the Province of Ontario.
At the same time, what has been the federal Government's response? Looking specifically at the question of acid rain, we see that the federal Government in its own intuitive nature has decided to appoint a dollar a year man, who is overpaid at that, in the person of the former Premier of Ontario. While this person was the Premier of the Province of Ontario-and 1 see the Hon. Member for Parry Sound-Muskoka (Mr. Darling) here, the issue crosses Party lines and concerns all Members-he was responsible for the sulphur dioxide emissions from Ontario Hydro, a Crown corporation. Ontario Hydro is one of the heaviest contributors to the acid rain problem in the Province of Ontario. The Premier chose to turn his back on the problem to protect Ontario Hydro and encouraged the belching of sulphur dioxide into the air by refusing to demand that stacks be properly equipped with scrubbers to prevent further emissions and further continuation of acid rain falling on the Ontario environment. But what does this person get as a reward for his decision to allow Ontario Hydro to pollute not only our air but also to create acid rain in the thousands of pounds? He is appointed the federal Government's envoy to the United States to deal with the American Government on the issue. He is to convince the Americans, in particular the President, who is reluctant to recognize that there is a problem that acid rain is an international problem demanding international solutions and a specific commitment on both sides of the Great Lakes.
I would suggest that his powers of persuasion will be rather muted in light of his own record when Premier of the Province of Ontario. He had an opportunity to do something but did nothing and sat aside without calling Ontario Hydro to task for polluting the air and for the acid rain problems which were directly the result of sulphur dioxide emissions from coal-fired generating stations which Ontario Hydro continues to use.
A number of questions have been raised by constituents, by mothers breast-feeding their children, by older men and women who feel they might be particularly vulnerable when the water quality is not as it could be. What we have seen from the Government, notwithstanding the rhetoric, the press conferences, the mutual meetings between Canada and the United

States, which looked very positive at first blush, is a Government, a Minister of the Environment, and the Minister's predecessor, that have stood by and done nothing while the slasher in the person of the Deputy Prime Minister as well as the President of the Treasury Board have torn the guts out of the long-term environmental studies and long-term environmental programs which would have allowed us to come to grips with the problem.
If the current Minister were serious about his mandate, one of the first things he should do is to seek in the next Budget an immediate reinstatement of the herring-gull program. This would give the people on the Great Lakes an indication of just what is happening to the quality of water, something all of us hold very dear.
Without that assurance, Mr. Speaker, and with the Government's continual refusal to take its own responsibility when it comes to research, research that could be done by the Guelph Toxicology Centre, we are sacrificing the long-term interests and the long-term health of our citizens for short-term economic deficit slashing and short-term private sector gain.
We have only to look at the so-called advice that was given by the Deputy Prime Minister in his addendum to the Wilson Economic Statement of November 9, 1984, when he examined the kinds of research to be funded by the Government. He said that he wanted fewer researchers, and more specific, immediate results from that research.
If that were the mandate given to those involved in developing the Salk vaccine, it is possible we would never have had the vaccine simply because the bottom line did not show up in the first year, the second year, the third year or the fourth year.
The analogy could be made, albeit somewhat removed, in the context of the Government's decision to privatize and sell off to a foreign corporation the de Havilland corporation at all costs. I believe, Mr. Speaker, that the people of Canada are prepared to fund, not only at current levels but more generously, programs which deal with the environment and research which can lead us to making this place liveable for our children.
The Member for Essex-Windsor (Mr. Langdon) called the environment a garbage dump. I think that analogy bears some study. Not only do we have municipalities across Canada that are not in a position to deal with their own solid waste other than to dump it directly into major rivers, but we also have toxic chemicals being disposed of illegally in many cases and in a fashion which can leech into the ground and affect directly

Supply
the water quality of many areas, like the riding of Hamilton East and the Windermere basin.
We know that some of the problems that arose from the Windermere basin were directly the result of the immoral activities of companies prepared to dump toxic waste without any bills of lading and without any proper and legal manifests simply because they wanted to get rid of what could be a highly toxic chemical. They were not prepared to spend the money they should have spent to dispose of it.
Unfortunately, if we as a Government say we will leave our environmental problems up to the private sector, then once again we are giving to them a role which should be a role taken by Government. The private sector is not in a position to develop the kind of research programs that will tell us 10 or 15 years down the road what action we must take to prevent the contamination of our water supply system.
With respect to the issue of the St. Clair River-the infamous blob as it has come to be known across the country-we have seen a number of factors which have impinged upon the situation to create a climate of fear and uncertainty for the area residents. We have also seen some concerns with respect to their very health and, indeed, the potential of carcinogenic materials as they directly relate to the constituents.
1 think the people of Canada are prepared to see more funds set aside in the Budget and the adoption of more stringent regulations as they relate, for example, to automobile emissions. I say this because the people of Canada are ahead of our politicians when it comes to the development of a system of clean water and air supply. I say that coming from the most industrialized riding in Canada with such heavy industry as that which takes place at the Steel Company of Canada, Dofasco, and many of the minor, secondary industries which spin off and develop their products as a result of the primary industry. The residents of Hamilton East are prepared to say: "Yes, we want to see more budget money spent on the environment. We want to see more budget money devoted to the study of those herring gull eggs. We want to know what is happening to individuals and whether, in fact, unborn children will suffer potential birth defects as a result of the water we are drinking". People want to know, and they are prepared to pay the price for the knowledge.
The Minister involved said that the Government was faced with budget cuts and it had to deal with the past excesses of Liberal Governments. In fact, the long-term ramification of the decision to terminate or cut back government funding in these important areas is that 10 years hence we will not even be able to identify the problem, never mind seek solutions. In fact, most thinking people-and I believe most Canadians have given this particular matter serious consideration-will recognize that it is in the best economic interest of Hamilton East. It is in the best economic interest of Ontario and of Canada to begin to adopt strategies and approaches which will not only identify the problem through government-led research but which will also develop solutions. That means some tough
legislation, such as the Ontario spills Bill which the Liberal Government of Ontario was prepared to introduce. It means some tough negotiations at the federal level. It means we have to appoint negotiators who are prepared to go in and fight for the rights of Canada, not simply appoint one-dollar-a-year people who are using the office as a camouflage for their own private activities and their own directorships. We know from statements which have been made by the Canadian Coalition on Acid Rain that there are some real concerns about the role the Canadian negotiator has played in the whole issue and whether or not he is really committed and fighting for Canada.
We must address some of the most difficult questions, for example, that of water quality. We know that water pollution is now costing us hundreds of millions of dollars a year in economic losses. This is because, in many areas, surface water will not be fit for household consumption, recreation or even industrial use until extensively treated. So there is the cost of treatment to be considered. Also, there is the fact that water quality in many areas appears to be declining. Unfortunately, I think many Canadians are of the belief that the St. Clair River situation is not an isolated case. I believe the Hon. Member for Davenport put the question well in this respect.
We can also look to the Niagara River near the great metropolis of Hamilton in the Niagara fruit belt in this regard. The Niagara River has become the receptacle for industrial chemical toxic substances which have, in fact, led to the discovery of more dioxins. A little more than a year ago in the riding of Hamilton East dioxin trace contaminants were found in the air emitting from one of our local sewage treatment facilities.
It seems to me that this is not simply a question of the St. Clair River and the blob. The blob is an example of what happens when a Government turns its back on research. That is what happens when a Government states, as this Government has stated: "We don't have time for research with respect to the herring gull program. We don't have the time to look at water quality from the public perspective. We will leave it to the private sector". The private sector has a role to play; but in this particular case it is the federal Government, in co-operation with provincial and municipal Governments, which should be taking the lead, in concert with companies which are prepared to share the burden. Frankly, with respect to an issue which concerns every Canadian, the leadership role should come from the federal Government.

subtopic: PUBLIC SERVICE-SMOKING IN THE WORKPLACE. (B) REQUEST FOR LEGISLATION
PUBLIC SERVICE-SMOKING IN THE WORKPLACE. (B) REQUEST FOR LEGISLATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on January 17 I asked extremely important questions of the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. de Cotret) and the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Epp) regarding the right of employees to have clean air at their place of work. The President of the Treasury Board replied as follows:
-we have indeed come to an agreement with the unions to ensure that all employees will be able to work in a healthy environment.
He thought that the tribunal which had ruled in favour of an employee, Peter Wilson, who had taken a grievance to it, had gone too far because this tribunal had ruled in favour of the employee and in favour of the right to have clean air at the place of work. However, the President of the Treasury Board said:
-this Government and the Treasury Board want all our employees to work in a healthy environment.
If that were true, I would indeed be happy. Since then I have received a letter from the Public Service Alliance of Canada which has been supporting this employee in his grievance. This is the devastating reply to the comments of these two Ministers, and I quote:
I must take this opportunity to correct the misconceptions that the President of the Treasury Board and the Minister of National Health and Welfare have left. It is correct that the Public Service Alliance of Canada and other public service unions negotiated "Smoking Guidelines". There is ample documentation and correspondence which passed between the unions and the employer to demonstrate that it was the employer who blocked at every step of the way any attempt to put in place significant controls on smoking in the work place. The guidelines which I have attached are watered down beyond recognition from what the public service unions, and particularly the Public Service Alliance, originally put forth as a smoking guideline. Unfortunately, this was the most we could extract from the employer.
I have the guidelines and it is very clear what the Government had to say and what those on the staff side wanted. The staff wanted a clean working environment and the government did not give a damn, being perfectly content in deciding that smokers have the right to pollute the working environment and non-smokers have the right to put a little sign up saying "bad air, please go away". Of course, we know all too well that

February 3, 1986
Adjournment Debate
these kinds of regulations are totally ineffective. However, PSAC and other unions have vigorously put forward very sane and sensible proposals for decent air at the workplace and protection for all of their employees, and separate provisions for smoking employees in areas which are separately ventilated. This is what all of the experts tell us is absolutely essential if we are going to have a genuine safe place of work.
The report of the tribunal which ruled in favour of Peter Wilson is quite interesting. It is quite shameful when we see the stance the Government is taking, actually bringing in an expert to argue that lung cancer has not really killed all that many passive smokers. How many thousands of deaths does the Government want before it will take this problem seriously? We have plenty of evidence of its seriousness. There are
35.000	deaths in Canada a year from tobacco-related diseases,
5.000	of whom have been passive smokers. Is that not enough deaths for Treasury Board to take some action?
There have been all kinds of ridiculous discussions about what a dangerous substance is and it has been suggested that tobacco smoke has really not been proven to be dangerous. It sounds like the tobacco companies which, over the last 20 years, tried to argue that tobacco smoke does not cause lung cancer, heart disease or emphysema. It is an absolutely shameful exhibition on the part of the Government.
There was a very sad grievance by Mr. Tinpower of Air Canada, an employee who is trying to get clean air at his place of work. In fact, it was ruled that he was not in "imminent" danger. We know that lung cancer, emphysema and all kinds of bronchial ailments are not caused instantly. Therefore an employee cannot claim "imminent" danger. It is not as if there is some unsafe condition where some piece of equipment is going to fail apart and kill someone. However, we do know that tobacco smoke does cause death in very large numbers. To say that because it will not do so in the next 10 minutes somehow makes this danger any more acceptable is being very shortsighted indeed. I think this goes to show that what we need is adequate legislation which does not confine "dangers" to dangers which happen in the next 10 minutes but long-term dangers such as lung cancer, emphysema and heart disease.
The Canadian Medical Association Journal is very clear on this subject, and I quote:
The sidestream smoke that both smokers and nonsmokers are forced to inhale from an "idling" cigarette may contain 40 times more of some potent carcinogens, such as N-nitrosodimethylamine, than the mainstream smoke that smokers willingly draw into their lungs. Indeed, smokers may be at even greater risk than nonsmokers from the carcinogens in sidestream smoke.
An article in the Canadian Medical Association Journal contains very clear recommendations as to what the Government should be doing in response to the seriousness of this problem, and I quote:
The current patchwork legislation that aggregates smokers in public places and still allows them to pollute the common airspace must be superseded by a master plan for a smoke-free indoor environment. Legislation must oblige employers, merchants and transport companies to provide smoke-free environments for anyone who is not smoking.
This is only elementary common decency. Unfortunately, the Minister of National Health and Welfare has been loath to
take any kind of action whatsoever. He talks about co-operation with the unions, but they have to push to get even the most insipid kind of guidelines passed. The Minister has been asked to take action here on the Hill because we have a very poor working environment. My own employees have complained to me that they are forced, in doing work for me, to work in places which are unsafe for their health. The Minister of National Health and Welfare has not been willing to take any action whatsoever. It is time that we had some action. Employees deserve the right to a smoke-free environment. We know that the dangers are, and these polite decisions on the part of Government-that it is a matter of cosy negotiations, and it does not come through when it is asked-is not enough.

speakeroldname: Mr. Paul Dick (Parliamentary Secretary to President of the Treasury Board):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Treasury Board
subtopic: PUBLIC SERVICE-SMOKING IN THE WORKPLACE. (B) REQUEST FOR LEGISLATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, 1 am sure that Hon. Members are aware that the guidelines on minimizing the effects of tobacco smoke in federal workplaces have been approved by the Treasury Board and were issued to all Public Service departments and agencies one year ago, in February of 1985. These guidelines were initially developed by a joint committee of Treasury Board Secretariat and Health and Welfare Canada officials, and were subsequently submitted to the National Joint Council of Public Service Unions, which is the official forum for consultation between the employer and public service unions. It was agreed by officials of Treasury Board, Health and Welfare Canada and the National Joint Council that the application of these guidelines would be based, principally, upon courtesy and consideration between smokers and non-smokers.
Through these guidelines, Departments are directed to develop and publish their own detailed internal departmental policies on smoking in the workplace in consultation with their employees. This policy of consultation, rather than acting as a dictator, is an essential requirement for ensuring the development and successful application of an internal policy that will achieve the intent of minimizing the effects of tobacco smoke in the workplace.
Departmental policies must, however, include the designation of certain areas as non-smoking areas, such as elevators, stairwells, change rooms, computer rooms, clinics, health units, service wickets and counters, and any other locations where the public is served. Departments may also designate all or part of cafeterias, waiting rooms and lounges as non-smoking areas. Unless there is consensus among the participants, smoking is not to be permitted during meetings.
Other areas in the workplace may be designated as nonsmoking or smoking areas through local consultation and agreement. "No Smoking" signs or symbols are to be made available for installation in all designated non-smoking areas. Employer and union participants in the National Joint Council recognize that these guidelines are an important first step in addressing this issue. However, it has been agreed by both parties that within a prescribed period of time, further joint consultation will take place to upgrade the guidelines to give effect to more stringent requirements. In fact, the National
February 3, 1986

Joint Council is beginning consultation on the present policy guidelines with the view to reviewing and upgrading the guidelines into a standard of smoking in the workplace.
These consultations will take place with the benefit of direct input of health experts of Health and Welfare Canada who are represented in the National Joint Council in the Standing Committee of that forum which reviews and makes recommendations concerning occupational safety and health and physical working conditions within the Public Service of Canada. I am sure that the joint input of health professionals, employee and departmental representatives will evolve in the development of an appropriate and practicable standard which, when implemented, will respond to this important issue.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to make a few comments about the property and casualty insurance business in Canada. On January 14, 1986, I asked the Minister of State for Finance (Mrs. McDougall) what the Government planned to do in conjunction with her provincial counterparts to help the crisis which has overtaken the insurance industry. 1 would hope that both levels of Government will go about analysing this situation in a calm and reasoned way.
When I spoke earlier on this topic, I mentioned the outlandishly high claims which are taking over this industry. Those claims, of course, result in soaring premium rates. I made the point that I hoped we did not become the California of the North. We have to work on this with other levels of Government because we have different responsibilities in this regard. The federal responsibility is to ensure that federally-regulated companies are solvent. I understand the Minister has some further steps to take in this regard.
I think the industry's problems can be summarized in three categories: availability; affordability; and solvency. I need not remind people that this industry is one of the most competitive in the country. As I understand it, no one company has as much as 10 per cent of market share. 1 think the largest has 8 per cent. I also think it is true to say that over the last number of years Canadians have been able to obtain insurance at some very reasonable rates, thanks to the aggressive tactics of hundreds and hundreds of general insurance agents. I have a couple of friends in this business in my own riding, Gordon Grant and Don Bell. They have been in the business for a number of years and share my concern that some steps have to be taken.
I would like to highlight some of the trends which have developed in this industry. As of the end of 1984 there were 243 regulated companies under federal jurisdiction in Canada. Another 77 companies are registered under various provincial jurisdictions. It is no secret this industry goes in cycles. It has had good times and not so good times. The industry's profits come from two sources. One is the underwriting profit, which
Adjournment Debate
is the difference between claims and earned premiums. The other is investment income. Between 1983 and 1984, while written and earned premiums increased $300 million, claims increased by $700 million.
The industry paid out $1.10 for every dollar of earned premium. However, in the liability section, which is where most of the problems have been, the industry paid out $1.38 for every dollar of premium earned. That has to have a dramatic and negative effect in several areas. One of those areas is the return on equity, or the return to the investor. That has gone from 9.4 per cent in 1982 to 10.9 per cent in 1983, and then a drastic drop to 1.2 per cent in 1984. We have not seen the 1985 results as yet but I am quite sure they will be just as bad as 1984.
Court claims are of particular concern to a number of people in the industry, as well as the average Canadian. A youngster in Brampton was awarded over $6 million just recently. There was a large award recently to a couple whose grandchild was the victim. In a good number of cases these claims are very valid, but when they are larger, two things happen. We all have to pay higher premiums to start with. In some cases the claims are so astronomical that the companies themselves cannot even begin to measure the risk inherent in a given type of coverage and therefore they back out of the whole market. Then no one can get insurance at any cost. We have seen that happen to a number of groups over the past few weeks, including our national ski team. There are also day care centres, school boards, municipalities and others who are running the risk of having no insurance at all. The Hon. Member for Mississauga South (Mr. Blenkarn) proposed that the federal Government put together a reinsurance package. That may be necessary, Mr. Speaker, because I gather that the world-wide capacity for reinsurance has dropped by a factor of about 75 per cent in just the last year or two.
Affordability is another key problem. People want insurance, but at what cost? The St. John's Ambulance group, which I mentioned in my previous remarks, saw its annual premium for liability go from $16,000 for $2 million of liability insurance coverage to $205,000 for $1 million of coverage.
Another specific example is that of a 20-year old trying to insure a 1979 Malibu for $250 deductible collision insurance and $500,000 liability insurance. He took the pro driving course and is a university student. In his case the insurance was going to cost $2,228. Something is out of control when we have premiums like this.
I would like to summarize, Mr. Speaker, by saying that this industry has had its cycles. The executives and leaders in that industry feel that they will work through it. The solvency aspect, which is the responsibility of the federal Government, is critical in this case. If people pay these premiums and have a claim, we must ensure that they are able to collect. I have confidence that this issue is getting a good amount of attention at all levels of Government. I do not believe we need strong

February 3, 1986
Adjournment Debate
government intervention in this. We do not need a knee-jerk reaction. We do not need the Government to set rates. This is a very competitive area and I think the market-place will render the proper premiums. Therefore, while I encourage each level of Government to take on its responsibilities, let us do it in a calm and reasonable way for the benefit of all Canadians.

speakeroldname: Mr. G. M. Gurbin (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of the Environment):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of the Environment
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to thank the Hon. Member for Don Valley East (Mr. Attewell) for his very informed comments. It is clear that this issue has touched individuals and groups and communities of Canadians across the country. It is becoming an increasing concern for both them and the Government.
The Member for Don Valley East has ascribed the main problem to the level of court awards. While this is one aspect of the issue, the Minister is aware that there are other aspects and other considerations, some of which the Member touched on. In addition to court awards, I think the situation is also caused by poor operating results in companies, fear on the part of the industry about the uncertainty of future liability awards, and by a significant tightening of the reinsurance market as the Member mentioned. Of course, all the factors are interrelated and the situation is not confined only to Canada but is evident in other countries as well.
The Hon. Member asks what the federal Government will do to limit the costs. He has also indicated his desire not to have the Government become too directly involved. At the same time, I think we should establish very clearly the levels of responsibility. Since reform of the law of tort is not under federal jurisdiction, we must leave this aspect to the province. On the other hand, we do have responsibility with regard to the solvency standards and regulatory requirements.
One thing which should be noted is that the Province of Ontario, which has the responsibility for any direct changes, has indicated that there will be a task force. We have indicated that the federal Minister will co-operate fully with that task force and is prepared to assist in any way possible. The Minister thought she could be particularly helpful in the areas of solvency standards, the area in which the federal Government has some jurisdiction. A considerable amount of work has already been done in this area.
In closing, Mr. Speaker, the Government will press ahead with legislation with regard to strengthening the solvency standards and regulatory requirements for insurance companies. The objective is to promote financial stability which, in turn, should encourage new capital and better availability of reinsurance which would ease capacity problems and stabilize the premiums paid by customers.

subtopic: ENVIRONMENTAL AFFAIRS-PROPOSED GUELPH TOXICOLOGY CENTRE. (B) MINISTER'S POSITION
ENVIRONMENTAL AFFAIRS-PROPOSED GUELPH TOXICOLOGY CENTRE. (B) MINISTER'S POSITION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on November 4 I asked the Minister of the Environment (Mr. McMillan) about the future of the Toxicology Centre in
Guelph which had been scrapped by the Conservative Government in November of 1984. I inquired whether he would be willing to reverse that decision. As reported on page 8322 of Hansard, he indicated to the House: "I am not even sure it is true that the Government has cancelled the plan for the Toxicology Centre ... That proposal still stands."
On December 14, when approached in Toronto by Christie MacLaren of The Globe and Mail, the same Minister is quoted as saying: "I am first of all subject to Government restraint and I have to work within that. I cannot expect the Department of the Environment to be totally exempted from such Government austerity". He was replying to a question related to the Toxicology Centre in Guelph and seemed to indicate that he was not sure whether such a centre would receive financing.
We in the Opposition would like to see the Government take a clear position. Where does that centre stand at the present time? Is it, as the Minister said on November 4, a proposal that still stands and, if so, when will an announcement be made and what will be the nature of that announcement? Is it a matter that the Minister put aside, as he did one month later, claiming that he has to be subject to the restraints of the Government?
It is very difficult to accept its reasoning on toxic chemicals and the necessity to put a centre aside on the basis of restraint because the first thought that comes to mind is whether the Government puts the health of Canadians in second place. 1 am sure the Parliamentary Secretary would be the last one who would want to assert that proposition. However, it is hard to believe that the Government would still vacillate on this matter in light of what has happened in recent months.
Let me draw the attention of the Parliamentary Secretary to the study that was published in December. It is a one-year report from the Royal Society of Canada and the United States National Research Council which concluded that the 37 million people living in the Great Lakes region ingest more toxic chemicals through their food and drinking water than anyone else on the continent. The scientists are reported as saying that they are concerned about the unknown long-term effects that minute amounts of many toxic chemicals may have on human health. The scientists are recorded as calling for an urgent clean-up of the many sources of air and water pollution, but also for research into the nature of the chemicals themselves and how they affect human health. However, when this report was announced in December, the recommendations for research came a year after the Government announced Budget cuts ending numerous studies on how pesticides and other toxic chemicals affected wildlife and after plans were scrapped to build the Guelph Toxicology Centre.
It seems that the Government does not know how to make up its mind and that we have a Minister who is giving vague answers just for the sake of keeping alive a hope, without really giving an indication as to what we might expect in the future. I find that kind of behaviour reprehensible because I
February 3, 1986

believe the Canadian public and the scientific community are entitled to have an answer now. This has been dragging for too long. If the decision on December 4, 1984, when the centre was scrapped still stands, say so. However, do not raise false hopes with a statement in the House on November 4, 1985, then make a statement in Toronto which seems to wipe out every hope. The subject matter is too important for this kind of political game. I am sure that the Parliamentary Secretary, in his straightforward manner, will want to remove the doubts and come clean with the Opposition on that matter on behalf of his Minister.
Evidently, the question behind all this is one which has been in our minds all day long-when will the Government come to its senses and realize that the economy is in danger when environmental research is cut, dropped or given up? Research and better knowledge and information on toxic chemicals in this part of the industrialized world in North America mean in practical terms the protection of our water and the protection of our health because we all depend upon water. In the long term it also means the protection of the viability of our economy because water is obviously an essential element. If the substances in water are not understood, and if we cannot take remedial action because we do not understand clearly what is going on, in the long term we will certainly pay.
I am sure the Parliamentary Secretary has a very clear reply on the Guelph Toxicology Centre.

speakeroldname: Mr. G. M. Gurbin (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of the Environment):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of the Environment
subtopic: ENVIRONMENTAL AFFAIRS-PROPOSED GUELPH TOXICOLOGY CENTRE. (B) MINISTER'S POSITION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, there is no question that in the long run we will all pay for our sins, whatever they are. I have not read the comment which the Hon. Mmember quoted
Adjournment Debate
from a Toronto newspaper, so I am not sure whether that newspaper report is precisely true. I certainly see no confusion in what I understand compared with what the Minsiter said in the House. To make it very clear for the Hon. Member, he knows full well that the funds for the toxicology centre were cancelled in the November 8 statement. He has already been told enough times the rationale for that. Quite clearly it was to take a look in a comprehensive fashion at our research policy.
We have four toxicology research centres in Canada- Laval, Sherbrooke, Saskatoon and Vancouver. We have had three assessments of our research activities in Canada. One was conducted through Environment Canada, one through the National Research Council, and one through the Science Council of Canada. Those reports have in fact been completed. However, for the purposes of clarification-and I do not know whether the Hon. Member will be satisfied-the proposal as such has never gone away. There are people who continue to be very interested and there are people who have been actively working on that proposal and have made representations which the Government is seriously considering and looking at, in light of the modification of the representations and in light of the assessments which have been made on toxicology research right across the country. It is an example of a comprehensive look at a situation which we in government consider to be of utmost importance and which we intend to satisfy with a national water policy. In many areas of Government we have taken an active role and have displayed active leadership. We intend to continue.
